10037-a-beautiful-possibility:
Edith Ferguson Black's novel opens on one of the fairest West Indian islands, where a simple but elegant villa lifts its gabled roofs among tropical beauty. Brilliant birds move in the foliage, gold and silver fish dart in a fountain basin, and hammocks hang on the vine-shaded veranda.

Into this beauty comes a story of love and possibility, suggested by its title and by a frontispiece of a man dashing a glowing cigar end in another's face. Black writes a warm island romance, where passion meets the manners of a small colonial world. Readers get sunshine, feeling, and a heroine's chance at happiness.
10147-america-s-war-for-humanity:
Thomas H. Russell compiled this pictorial history of the First World War, praising American troops and the cause of liberty. The book leans on official photos and captions, rather than long narrative, to carry its case. Its tone is openly patriotic, written soon after the fighting for a home audience.

Pictures show machine-gun teams, artillery crews, Chateau Thierry after battle, trench grenades, and the surrender of the German fleet. Each image pairs a scene with a short, proud note on American courage. Readers get a vivid, period album of the war as Americans first chose to remember it.
10468-aunt-jane-s-nieces-in-society:
Edith Van Dyne published this girls' novel in 1910, sending Patsy, Beth, and Louise into society under Uncle John's duty to do right by them. Mrs. Merrick scolds John Merrick for neglecting the girls, while he gazes at the rug, calm and chubby, in an elaborate morning scene. The tone is comic and bright.

A question of pull, Diana, the Von Taer pearls, a limousine, and Madame Cerise, custodian, carry the plot through misled hopes, fog, and a crisis. A telephone call and the unexpected bring matters to a head. Readers get a lively series tale of social climbing, mystery, and friendship.
10522-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-04:
John Lord published this fourth volume of Beacon Lights of History, on imperial antiquity, treating great empires through great men. Lord, author of The Old Roman World and Modern Europe, writes lectures that join narrative to moral judgment. The volume moves from Persia to Rome with broad, readable strokes.

Cyrus the Great opens the set, with Persian religion, civilization, and conquests, from Lydia and Babylon to the fall of the empire under later kings. Julius Caesar follows, as an instrument of providence and imperialism. Readers get a vivid, old-style history of ancient empire by biography.
10557-johnny-crow-s-party:
L. Leslie Brooke drew this second Johnny Crow picture book in 1907, following Johnny Crow's Garden of 1903. Brooke dedicates it to his nephew Somerset, happy in a name that assures welcome to any party. Johnny Crow plies rake and hoe and improves his little garden, while animal guests arrive in fine form.

An eagle looks regal, a cockatoo asks in French how you do, a gander fails to understand, and a flamingo talks the same lingo. A bear sings a sentimental air at the tea in the garden. Readers get a delightful, rhymed picture book, beloved for its animals, verses, and drawings.
11065-aunt-mary-s-primer-adorned-with-a-:
Aunt Mary's Primer, published in 1851 with one hundred and twenty pretty pictures, teaches young children to read by whole words, not letter names. A note to teachers advises pronouncing monosyllables at once, such as am and as, and syllables separately in longer words, such as car-pet and po-ker. Spelling lessons can wait; quick reading comes first.

Lessons name things in the room, the senses, colours, months, and country employments, with pictures of ploughing, reaping, haymaking, mills, and churches. Children learn July heat, August harvest, September apples, and December Christmas. The primer closes with a little poem to learn by heart. It shows Victorian methods of first reading, visual, practical, and short.
11470-his-big-opportunity:
Amy Le Feuvre's 1898 children's book His Big Opportunity opens on a garden wall, where two boys in white cricketing flannels debate making an opportunity happen. Below stretches an old-fashioned English garden in August sun, dogs asleep on the lawn, a gardener smoking by a wheelbarrow, and an old stone house behind creepers. Chapters follow a song, a lost donkey, Rob, a walnut story, the Bertrams' leap, a cripple, a gift to the queen, letters, old Principle, heroes, and a boy's big opportunity.

Le Feuvre, author of Probable Sons and Teddy's Button, writes moral adventure for children, where initiative and kindness create chances. The book's sunny opening sets its tone. Young readers will find its heroes earnest and its lessons gently worn.
12082-color-images-from-mars-rovers-spir:
Bob Webster assembled this short illustrated work from public NASA images taken by the Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity. The rovers cameras shot mostly in black and white, so Webster combined frames taken through different color filters into full-color views.

Short captions explain each scene: rock outcrops at Meridiani Planum, the El Capitan region, dust magnets on the rover decks, and plains scattered with small disc-shaped cavities. Webster notes where color is approximate, since filter sets, sun angles, and minutes between frames can shift shadows. The result is a plain, useful guide to what the early rover panoramas actually showed of the Martian surface.
12349-the-secret-city:
Hugh Walpole published The Secret City in 1919, a novel in three parts set in revolutionary Russia. Walpole, author of Fortitude and The Dark Forest, knew Petrograd from wartime service, and the book draws on that experience.

The narrator moves among English residents, Russian friends, and revolutionaries, visiting Henry Bohun and advising kindness toward Nicholas Markovitch. The secret city of the title is Petrograd itself, beautiful and menacing, where loyalties shift daily. Walpole writes with atmosphere and sympathy for Russians caught in upheaval. The novel is a vivid outsider view of revolution, less political than personal, and it remains one of Walpole best-known works.
12557-the-penalty:
Gouverneur Morris's 1913 novel, The Penalty, illustrated by Howard Chandler Christy, opens with a wistful question: are you in love with me now? A dedication to Mary Baldwin recalls a shared Iliad, a turkey carved at her right hand, and tit-bits and oyster falling to the narrator. Hector fixed Achilles in their childhood play.

The novel that follows, a romance of crime, revenge and a man without legs who rules an underworld, turns on penalty paid in body and soul. Morris writes in a popular, melodramatic manner, with Christy's illustrations heightening the romance. The book became a well-known early twentieth-century thriller, later filmed, and it shows Morris at his most sensational.
12643-twenty:
Stella Benson's 1918 poems, Twenty, dedicated in spirit to youth, open with Christmas 1917, a key no thief can steal, a faery door adventurous and golden, a palace perfect to our eyes. Has the past died before present sin, the poem asks, has this cruel age stoned to martyrdom that magic day enthroned within those halls?

No, the poem answers, through young spring rain, faint summer and autumn burning, our still immortal day has heard again our steps returning. Contents run from The Secret Day and songs through The Orchard, Words, Redneck's Song and To the Unborn. The Newer Zion, Two Women Sing, The Woman Alone, The Dog Tupman, Saint Bride and Five Smooth Stones follow. Benson writes lyrical, wartime verse, wistful and resilient.
12659-the-vertical-city:
Fannie Hurst's 1922 stories, The Vertical City, open with She Walks in Beauty, Back Pay, the title story, The Smudge, Guilty and Roulette. She Walks in Beauty compares a New York hotel to the Taj Mahal. As Jehan at Agra raised a tomb for a dead wife, so the Bon Ton hotel rears fourteen stories of elegantly furnished suites, all comforts and none of the discomforts of home.

An Indiana-limestone and Vermont-marble tomb to Hestia, the hotel charges sixty dollars a week and up, asking guests to leave fireside talk behind. Hurst writes about city women, money, love and work, with sharp, sympathetic detail. The collection captures Jazz Age New York, vertical, crowded and bright, through stories of its rooms and streets.
12946-the-boy-scouts-on-picket-duty:
Robert Shaler's Boy Scouts on Picket Duty follows Hugh and his troop along the Florida coast, where the sloop Arrow carries a startling message to Key West. Captain Lemuel Vinton, twelve miles northeast of Key West at Snipe Point, turns back from a cruise to warn authorities after an easterly squall. Smugglers, a beach hut, kidnapping, and a blazing beacon follow.

A pursuit scene finds the Arrow stuck on a sandbar, waiting for tide, while Hugh puzzles why no chase came after a stolen canoe. Branks's low whistle at the hut answers another whistle in the dark. The book blends scout work with coastal adventure.
12989-the-lady-of-big-shanty:
F. Berkeley Smith's 1909 novel takes its title from a camp in the Adirondack woods of New York, where city men go to hunt and fish. The story follows visitors drawn north for sport, among them a hunter named Thayor, and the people who live year-round in that rough country. Smith, who knew the woods well, writes the lakes, trails, and winter cold as forces in their own right.

At the center stands a woman caught between a husband, a doctor guest, and the pull of wild country itself. Hunting trips, long talks by the fire, and quiet jealousies slowly test each bond. The novel argues, in story form, that life stripped to food, fire, and shelter lays bare what fine manners hide. It also holds that the wild can change a mind more surely than any city talk.
13019-raphael-or-pages-of-the-book-of-li:
Alphonse de Lamartine's Raphael, in this 1905 illustrated edition, is a young man's record of first love, told as pages from the book of life at twenty. Lamartine, born at Mâcon in 1790, had known prison in his family, school at Belley, and travel in Italy before he wrote. The novel draws on that youth and on the France of his day.

Raphael loves Julie, a woman bound to another, and the pair choose self-denial over full happiness on earth. Lamartine turns their restraint into a claim for a purer union beyond life, in the realm of pure spirits. The prose is ardent and mournful by turns, and the book stands as a classic French romance of love renounced, not love won.
13104-the-abominations-of-modern-society:
Rev. T. De Witt Talmage's 1872 sermons, gathered as The Abominations of Modern Society, warn readers against the snares of city life. Talmage calls his book a buoy swung over rocks, meant to keep ships from a lee shore. His preface says the book is for young and old, men and women alike, and he praises good women while condemning bad ones in the plain style of his day.

Chapters lift the curtain on winter nights, the power of clothes, dancing after midnight, and the massacre by needle and sewing machine. One passage follows Salome's dance, with arms tossed and feet pulsing, until a king swears any gift she asks. Another tells of a lottery for an opera house, a swindle that left the building with its first owner. Talmage preaches with fire, story, and warning.
13715-the-history-of-the-fabian-society:
Edward R. Pease, secretary of the Fabian Society for twenty-five years, wrote its insider history. He traces Fabian socialism from the early 1880s, through Positivism, Henry George, Mill, Owen, and Marx. Early chapters cover ghost-hunting, Thomas Davidson's circle, and the Fellowship of the New Life. Later chapters follow the society's growth, tracts, and campaigns.

Pease writes with first-hand knowledge and dry humour. He names founders, quarrels, and turning points without hiding failures. The book explains gradualist socialism: reform by research, lectures, and local government, not revolution. It remains the standard early account of British Fabianism. Students of socialism and Labour history still start here.
1422-going-into-society:
This short Christmas piece follows a London house that falls into the hands of a showman, who fills it with wonders for paying visitors. Through the house's changing fortunes, the narrator traces a family story of pride, ruin, and return, with a ghostly hint that the past never quite leaves its rooms.

Told in a compact, anecdotal style, the tale mixes humour with a touch of the uncanny. Its showman and his exhibits give a comic frame to a sober theme. It is a small, odd seasonal story about houses, fortunes, and the crowds who pay to stare at other people's lives.
14780-evidences-of-christianity:
William Paley's Evidences of Christianity, in a new 1851 edition, argues the Christian case from history, testimony and the character of the apostles. Paley dedicates the work to James York, Bishop of Ely, recalling a Cambridge station offered to him five years earlier by a man he had never met.

Chapters build a legal-style case: witnesses, miracles, prophecy and the spread of the faith are weighed as evidence, not merely asserted. Paley's plain, tutor-like prose made the book a standard text for students and clergy. It remains a classic of natural theology and apologetics, valuable for readers who want the eighteenth-century argument for Christianity in its most orderly form.
14996-painted-windows-studies-in-religio:
A Gentleman with a Duster wrote The Mirrors of Downing Street. He studies religious character in Painted Windows, with an introduction by Kirsopp Lake and pictures by Emile Verpilleux, published by Putnam in 1922. A frontispiece shows Bishop Gore, and a Lowell epigraph frames the book.

Light coloured by reverend effigies, Lowell warns, is none the more respirable for being picturesque, and windows that cannot be opened may break, though painted with saints and martyrs. The author profiles church leaders as characters, not doctrines, seeking fresh air in religion. Painted Windows is a popular, gossipy and serious survey of Anglican personality after the war.
15169-the-bobbsey-twins-in-a-great-city:
Laura Lee Hope's Bobbsey Twins book sends the twins to a great city, with a frontispiece showing children delighted by a store camp. The series list runs from the twins at home and at school to Snow Lodge, a houseboat, and Blueberry Island. This volume adds city streets, shops, and crowds to their adventures.

Bert, Nan, Flossie, and Freddie explore, skate, and get into small scrapes, with a supper served at seven as one cozy set piece. Hope writes in a simple, cheerful style for young readers. The book offers old-fashioned family fun, with city sights seen through children's eager eyes.
15527-captivity:
M. Leonora Eyles, author of Margaret Protests, published this novel in 1922, dedicated to E. J. R-S. The dedication says that friend wrote the book as surely as Beatrice wrote the Vita Nuova for Dante. Talk with her taught Eyles that lives are a pathway for God's feet. It taught her that body, brain, and spirit form a trinity. Eyles signed the dedication at Bexhill-on-Sea in February 1920.

An opening reflection states the novel's theme. Man comes into life to seek and find his sufficient beauty, to serve and increase it, and to fight for it. He counts death as nothing while dying eyes still turn to it. Fear, dullness, indolence, and appetite stand against him, delaying and hampering his quest. Eyles writes a spiritual novel of captivity and freedom, where secret thoughts need a strong, austere censor, and love shapes a life.
15545-the-basis-of-morality:
Annie Besant, author of Mysticism and Initiation, published this short book on the basis of morality in Adyar, Madras, in 1915, with the Theosophical Publishing House. Five chapters test five foundations: revelation, intuition, utility, evolution, and mysticism. The book asks a practical question for educators and for every reader: on what bedrock can morals rest?

Besant opens by asking whether religion and morals must go together, and whether one can be taught without the other. France, she says, tried to answer with a dreary little catechism that made boys long to be wicked. Religions based on revelation, she notes, call right what the giver commands and wrong what he forbids. The book then weighs each basis in turn, seeking a test of right and wrong that stands against life's storms.
15580-the-rustlers-of-pecos-county:
Zane Grey published this western novel in 1914, opening in Sanderson, Texas, with a narrator who walks the main street after an early breakfast, watching for what might happen. A stage-coach stands full of passengers, though it does not go to Linrock, and another leaves for that point three days a week. Cowboy broncos stand hitched, and two buckboards catch the narrator's eye.

George Wright and Colonel Sampson come out of the hotel, and Wright pays off the cowboy Russ, saying Miss Sampson will not need him at the ranch any more. Russ protests: this is the first he has heard of it. Wright answers briefly, sorry, kid, that's it. Grey sets up a range war of rustlers, ranchers, and hired guns, where a dismissal on a hotel porch starts a fight over Pecos County cattle.
15623-jukes-edwards-a-study-in-education:
A. E. Winship published this study in education and heredity in Harrisburg in 1900, with R. L. Myers and Company. It is dedicated to William R. George, founder of the George Junior Republic, who taught America how to give neglected, unfortunate, and wayward boys and girls a chance to become industrious, virtuous, upright citizens. A preface calls making regenerates out of degenerates America's most important problem.

Chapters contrast two families: the Jukes, and Jonathan Edwards and his descendants. Education, Winship argues, is more than school weeks or reading and writing; it shapes character, industry, and patriotism, and tends to do away with vulgarity, pauperism, and crime. The study follows Edwards children, home training, Aaron Burr, and Timothy and William Edwards. It is a dated but influential work on heredity, schooling, and social reform.
15691-woman-in-modern-society:
Earl Barnes once taught European history in Indiana. Later he taught education at Leland Stanford Junior University. His study appeared in New York in 1912, from B. W. Huebsch. Barnes wrote Studies in Education and Where Knowledge Fails. He dedicates it to a woman of health and strength. She was reared by a wise mother, trained to earn her living, and university bred.

Eleven chapters run from what it means to be a woman and woman's heritage. They pass through women in education and the feminizing of culture. They reach the economic independence of women and women in industry. Political life, woman's part in it, and the modern family follow. Family life as a vocation and a conclusion close the book. Barnes writes a progressive case for suffrage, work, and education, centered on a woman who is an equal partner at home and a force in her community.
15741-the-little-colonel-s-house-party:
A children's novel by Annie Fellows Johnston, author of The Little Colonel, issued by L. C. Page and Company in Boston in 1907. Louis Meynell supplied the pictures. Lloyd, the Little Colonel, throws a house party for friends at her Kentucky home. Johnston writes with warmth for girls who loved the earlier books.

Guests arrive, games begin, and small quarrels and kindnesses fill the visit. The Colonel, proud and tender by turns, learns to share her home and her heart. Southern manners and country pleasures colour every chapter. The book delights as a gentle party tale: friendship, fun, and a heroine growing up before her readers' eyes.
1575-the-foundations-of-personality:
Abraham Myerson, a psychiatrist, writes on the foundations of personality, asking how body, mind, and social life combine to make character. The book draws on medicine, psychology, and everyday observation. Myerson, a Boston psychiatrist, wrote for doctors and for general readers alike.

Myerson argues against simple theories, stressing glands, nerves, habit, and environment together. The work suits readers of early twentieth-century psychology who want a sane, medical view of human nature. His foundations, body and habit together, resist any single cause for character. Myerson's sane, medical tone sets the book apart from wilder theories of its day.
15852-the-texan-star-the-story-of-a-grea:
A Texas novel by Joseph A. Altsheler, issued by Appleton-Century-Crofts in New York in 1912. The Texan Star opens the story that The Texan Scouts continues, following Ned Fulton and his friends. Altsheler, a prolific writer for boys, treats the Texas Revolution as a great fight for liberty. The tale stands complete in itself.

Ned rides, scouts, and fights through a rising war against Mexican rule. Friends, foes, and famous names crowd the road to the Alamo's shadow. Altsheler keeps history clear amid adventure. The novel works as stirring history for young readers: brave lads, a just cause, and a star rising over Texas.
16135-safe-marriage-a-return-to-sanity:
Ettie A. Rout's 1922 book, published in London by William Heinemann's medical list with a preface by surgeon Sir William Arbuthnot Lane, argues for sanity in marriage. Rout writes frankly about health, honesty, and safety between husband and wife, at a time when such topics were rarely discussed in print. Her title promises a return to common sense after years of silence and shame.

The book speaks to married couples, parents, and doctors, urging open talk and practical care over fear and ignorance. Its medical backing gave it weight in a fierce public debate about marriage and morals. Readers today can use it as a landmark in the history of sex education and women's health writing.
16938-pressure-resistance-and-stability-:
J. C. Meem wrote this American Society of Civil Engineers paper number 1174 on pressure, resistance, and stability of earth, with discussion by Thomson, Gregory, Perry, Goodrich, Pruyn, Carter, and Meem. It follows Meem's earlier paper on bracing trenches and tunnels, noting minor experiments on the arching of sand. This paper takes up earth pressures in more detail, with further experiments, and considers resistance and stability for piling, foundations, and pressure on subaqueous structures in soft ground.

Meem gives engineers practical formulas and test results, with discussion that probes his claims. The paper is technical, dense, and aimed at builders of trenches, tunnels, and foundations. Readers of civil engineering history will find a key early study of earth pressure, useful for its experiments and its debate.
17115-fruits-of-toil-in-the-london-missi:
This 1869 volume tells the early work of the London Missionary Society, from its hard start in the age of the French Revolution to stations across the seas. Money was scarce, churches were small, and doors in India, China, Africa, and the West Indies stayed shut for years. The South Seas opened first, and the book follows preachers, schools, and converts island by island.

Maps and sketches add place to the tale of toil, sickness, and slow gains. The writers speak with pride in the sowers and patience with setbacks, in the plain style of a society report. Modern readers will find a frank record of mission zeal and its costs, as told by its own friends in 1869.
17220-bohemian-society:
Lydia Leavitt's Bohemian Society gathers a country house circle near a city, led by a well-read lady who loves people with ideas. Artists, authors, religious seekers, spiritualists, philanthropists, and philosophers meet and speak freely, each airing views without restraint. A dreamer among them sketches a modern Utopia: a fertile valley ringed by mountains, where folk live content and no one is richer than a neighbor.

The book mixes talk, tale, and ideal schemes in the earnest style of its Canadian press. Its charm lies in the medley itself, and in the lady host who draws odd minds together. Readers who like Victorian talk novels and utopian dreams will find a curious, gentle book about minds at play.
17848-life-in-a-medi-val-city:
Edwin Benson, bachelor of arts, wrote this study of life in a mediaeval city. It is illustrated by York in the fifteenth century, with eight pictures. It was published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge and in New York by Macmillan in 1920. Contents open with the important factors affecting York's history: geographical position, military value, and political importance.

Appearance follows, covering church, state, and people, streets, highways, traffic, and Ouse Bridge. Buildings, dwelling houses, shops, inns, and guildhalls complete the picture. Readers get a clear, readable portrait of a late mediaeval English city. The book suits readers of urban history and of York.
18103-contemptible-by-casualty:
An author who signed himself Casualty wrote Contemptible in 1916, printed in Philadelphia by Lippincott and in London by Heinemann. The book is the sixth in the Soldiers' Tales of the Great War, and its title answers the Kaiser's slur on the British Expeditionary Force.

Chapters run from leaving England at midnight, with no cheers or bands, to Mons, the retreat, darkness, and St. Quentin. The subaltern narrator tells of march, fear, and comradeship in plain, soldier prose. It is a vivid, first-war memoir, and a proud reply to contempt, told by a man who was there.
18202-the-growth-of-thought-as-affecting:
William Withington published this philosophical treatise in 1851. Withington asks how the growth of thought shapes the progress of society, and he treats human life as a problem to be managed. Self-love, seen under a threefold aspect, stands at the center of his account, with three agencies offered for bettering the human condition.

Part one defines life and distinguishes intellectual culture from intellectual life. Part two weighs social institutions, political economy, the papacy, the Reformation, and republicanism. Part three turns to philosophy as educator of self-love, and part four to religion as the agency that supplies what the others lack. Readers get an earnest Victorian system, built to show how thought, rightly grown, might mend society.
19197-how-freckle-frog-made-herself-pret:
Charlotte B. Herr wrote this 1913 picture story about Freckle Frog, who longs to look pretty for Robin Redbreast's party, where her cousin Billy Bullfrog will sing. She envies Big Mary's blue silk dress with lace and begs the Morning Glory Ladies for one like it. Designs by Frances Beem fill the little book.

The Morning Glory Ladies, angry at missing an invitation, refuse, but Little Black Spider spins her fine lace all day and brings it next morning. A parasol still awaits her. Young readers get a sweet garden tale of vanity, kindness, and the friends who help when grand ladies will not.
1950-a-woman-of-thirty:
On a Sunday morning in early April 1813, when Parisians first enjoyed the year's bright days, a girl named Julie d'Aiglemont begins a life that this novel follows into her thirties. The novel follows Julie d'Aiglemont from a girl's early mistakes through marriage, motherhood, and the slow education of a woman's heart.

Balzac's title marks the age at which Julie, having dreamed idly of Arthur, finds her dream come true in a young Englishman's half-feminine face. The novel weighs that love against duty, family, and time. It is a study of a woman's inner life across decades, written with Balzac's usual attention to the small facts of money, rank, and feeling.
19697-by-what-authority:
Great Keynes, a quiet backwater village, anchors the opening of By What Authority. A traveler waits there, impatient, while a horse is shod. London's whirl lies twenty miles north of him. The Brighton road rushes eight miles east. Against that stillness, the novel sets its question of authority. The story is a historical romance of England's religious struggles.

The famous tale behind this title concerns a young Catholic in Elizabethan England. Faith and crown pulled subjects in opposite directions then. A village far from court could still feel that pull. The novel uses slow country scenes to build its world. Its question, who may command belief, ran through the age.
19732-the-eternal-city:
Hall Caine wrote this novel of Rome, under a New York imprint in the early nineteen hundreds. A boy of ten or twelve in tattered clothes, carrying an accordion like a sack, opens the tale. It retells the Holy Roman Empire in modern dress, with love, faith, and power at stake.

A later scene finds a woman tying a lock of hair with ribbon, drying her eyes, and parting at the sound of clocks and street rumble. Caine's grand romance was a bestseller of its day, and it still moves with old-fashioned sweep.
20002-alroy-the-prince-of-the-captivity:
Benjamin Disraeli published Alroy in 1833, a romance of the medieval Jewish East. Its hero is David Alroy, the Prince of the Captivity. Disraeli defends his supernatural machinery as Cabalistically correct. From the Spirits of the Tombs to Solomon's sceptre, he claims Hebrew tradition as authority. The novel follows a would-be messiah raising revolt in Persia. Baghdad and the caliph's court frame his rising.

Disraeli, of Jewish descent, made Alroy his one Jewish epic. The historical Alroy led a twelfth-century movement among Kurdish Jews. Disraeli turns him into a Byronic conqueror-poet. Politics, prophecy, and ambition fuse in the hero exactly as in the author. Later prime ministers rarely leave juvenilia this revealing. Alroy is Disraeli dreaming his own destiny eastward.
20032-northern-nut-growers-report-of-the:
Northern nut growers met, spoke, and kept records of their meetings, and one such report survives here. The pages include long lists of members and guests. Names from Washington appear again and again in the roll. Karl W. Greene and T. P. Littlepage are among those listed.

Reports like this one record who came, where they lived, and what the group did. They are plain records, not tales, and their value lies in names and dates. Growers, officials, and keen amateurs all took part in this shared work on nuts and trees.
20160-a-history-of-american-christianity:
Leonard Woolsey Bacon published A History of American Christianity in 1897. Bacon was a minister and church historian of wide learning. He notes how near God's plans came to defeat by human enterprise. Medieval Norse trips to North America now look like fact, he argues.

From those early probes, the book traces churches across the new nation. Colonies, revivals, and new sects all pass in ordered review. Bacon writes as an insider who still weighs proof with care. Readers get a full, dated survey of faith in America to his day.
20174-freedom-truth-and-beauty:
Edward Doyle published Freedom, Truth, and Beauty in 1921, a book of poems and praise. Doyle was known as the blind poet of Harlem in New York. A note urges readers to take up his Haunted Temple poems. There they may feel shame for past moods of distrust and discontent.

His verse turns on faith, sight beyond eyes, and hope in hard life. Blindness shapes his image as a poet who sees by inner light. The book mixes his poems with warm words from his admirers. Readers get a period voice of faith and grit from Harlem's streets.
20337-a-narrative-of-the-mutiny-on-board:
William Bligh wrote A Narrative of the Mutiny on Board His Majesty's Ship Bounty. Bligh sailed from Otaheite on April 4, 1789, with his cargo safe. He carried 1,015 fine bread-fruit plants in the highest state of health. Many other valuable fruits of that country filled the ship too.

Weeks of care had gone into collecting those plants for transport. Weeks later, his crew rose and set him adrift in an open boat. Bligh's own account defends his conduct and tells that famed voyage home. Readers get the captain's voice from history's most famous mutiny.
20606-the-magic-city:
E. Nesbit's The Magic City is a children's fantasy about a boy who builds a city and steps inside it. Philip Haldane and his sister live in a little red-roofed house in a little red-roofed town. They have a little garden, a little balcony, and a little pony in a little stable.

When his sister marries and life changes, Philip builds a great model city from books, toys, and household things. The city becomes real, and Philip must rule and rescue it. Nesbit mixes everyday childhood with true wonder, in the style that made her the founder of modern children's fantasy.
20612-fort-amity:
Arthur Quiller-Couch set his novel Fort Amity in Canada during the French and Indian War. In his preface he hopes his remarks will not seem too pompous for the story he tells. It is a story in which true love is crossed by a soldier's sense of honor.

The theme, he admits, is a variant on a great commonplace. Following his habit, he lets the incidents and the characters make their own impression. Around the frontier fort, war between empires presses on private hearts. Quiller-Couch, who signed himself Q, writes the tale with a poet's care for place and speech.
20708-a-son-of-the-city:
Herman Gastrell Seely's A Son of the City, published in 1917, is a story of boy life in Chicago. Its hero grows up on city streets, with school, gangs, jobs, and baseball for his world. The first chapter's heading promises the pattern: In Which Our Hero Goes Fishing.

The book opens before dawn. Startled from a sound sleep, the boy fumbles beneath the bed to throttle the alarm clock. He must silence its clamor before it wakes the rest of the household. Seely writes city boyhood from the inside, in an age when such everyday stories for boys were rare.
20856-ten-from-infinity:
A Monarch Books science fiction novel from January 1963, Ten From Infinity bears Ivar Jorgensen's name. Ralph Brillhart painted its cover for the paperback trade. The imprint promised works picked for merit and reading fun alike.

Ten beings from beyond space give this brisk tale its hook and title. Paul Fairman, who wrote as Jorgensen, filled it with pulp pace and twists. Strange doubles and hidden foes drive the plot at speed. The book is a neat slice of early 1960s paperback science fiction, built to grip on the first page and not let go.
20936-the-new-society:
Ending the proletarian state can be neared, argues The New Society, by wise laws on property and schooling. Curbs on inheritance rights stand chief among its tools named here. Strict state control, the writer holds, is not required for that end.

Graham Wallas, a Fabian thinker, probes how great societies strain the human mind. Schools, wealth, and modern scale fill his thought on reform without revolt. Wallas wrote for readers who wanted reform. He asks how minds like ours can run states so vast. The book is a work of social thought.
20958-life-in-the-medieval-university:
Logic by Aristotle, sums by Boethius, and Euclid's geometry ruled the medieval schools, Robert S. Rait notes. Ptolemy stands for astronomy, though mixed with kings of his name. Theology crowned the long course that followed the arts degree.

Life in the Medieval University shows how scholars lived, ate, fought, and learned. Paris, Oxford, and Bologna supply tales of gowns, towns, and riots. Rait writes with a scholar's ease on a world half monkish, half rowdy. Students today will know much of it still: debt, lodging hunts, and fierce pride in one's own school and its ways.
21048-just-patty:
Mae Mertelle's financier father takes a hit from Patty Wyatt in Jean Webster's Just Patty, from 1911. Patty's own father, a reform judge, spends his days jailing financiers, she retorts. Her grin turns the proud boast into a shared schoolgirl laugh.

Patty, of Daddy-Long-Legs fame in Webster's wider world, stars in these school tales. Pranks, classes, and chums at St. Ursula's fill the brisk chapters. Webster writes girls with wit, nerve, and warm hearts in equal share. Just Patty shows her at her lightest, a convent school romp by a teller who never talked down to her girls.
21305-a-dash-from-diamond-city:
Two young men are sent from Mafeking with important despatches for the general at Kimberley in George Manville Fenn's Boer War tale. Their road crosses Boer-held country in South Africa, with mishaps at every stage. A side plot follows illicit diamond dealing around the diamond city of the title.

Just before reaching Kimberley the riders are badly wounded and lie unconscious for a fortnight. The despatches, sewn into a filthy, blood-stained jacket, are feared thrown away before they are found safe. Fenn opens in a mud-walled, iron-roofed office with typewriter and pens scratching, then moves out into the veld, where the dash is won or lost.
21772-the-path-of-duty:
An American long settled in London writes out a story for a curious friend in this Henry James tale of 1885. The story concerns Ambrose Tester, and the narrator knew all the parties from the first. He promises a regular development and tells it by a red fire in the December fog. Sixteen years of London life have left him, he says, still sensitive to the city's strangeness.

The title names the tale's pressure: what people owe, and what owing costs them. James builds the story from observation, talk, and small social turns rather than big events. London's bigness and strangeness fill the frame. It is James in his early manner, a moral knot tied slowly in good company.
21839-sense-and-sensibility:
Two sisters stand at the heart of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, shown here in the 1902 Macmillan edition. One sister is ruled by sense, the other by feeling. Hugh Thomson's drawings, first issued in 1896, fill this printing. The Dashwoods have long been settled at Norland Park in Sussex when the tale begins. A death soon strips the family of home and income, and the sisters must make their way in a narrower world.

Elinor hides her heart while Marianne wears hers openly, and love tests both habits hard. Austen writes courtship as a study in character, with wit in every drawing room. Austin Dobson supplies the introduction. It is Austen's first published novel, and still one of her most loved.
21960-blue-bonnet-s-ranch-party:
A Texas girl takes her friends west in Blue Bonnet's Ranch Party, part of the Blue Bonnet series for girls, issued in 1912. Blue Bonnet's party rides in a private car and still finds the journey to Woodford the longest-seeming ever taken. The frontispiece watches her see the sun rise out of the prairie. Lela Horn Richards and Caroline E. Jacobs created the series, with this sequel written by C. E. Jacobs and Edyth Ellerbeck.

The series ran through Boston, housekeeping, and a debut before and after this ranch visit. Thirteen impressions by 1921 show how girls loved her. John Goss drew the pictures. The book gives its heroine both worlds: Boston polish and a Texas ranch, with the ranch winning the party's heart.
21981-the-essentials-of-spirituality:
What spirituality is, apart from any creed, is Felix Adler's question in The Essentials of Spirituality. Adler, founder of the Ethical Culture movement, begins with hunger: first the felt absence of spirituality, then the search for a higher quality of life. The quality, he argues, may come through belief in a divine father, through Spinoza's pantheism, through Buddhism's Nirvana, or through Ethical Culture itself.

He warns that the word spiritual often serves as a synonym for muddy thought and misty feeling. His remedy is definition joined to portraits of character. The essay is short, calm, and meant for seekers outside the churches. It shows Adler's lifelong project: keeping the moral fire of religion while letting its doctrines go. Few American sermons argue so gently.
22118-official-report-of-the-niger-valle:
Martin R. Delany, a Black abolitionist, doctor, and writer, led an exploring party to West Africa in 1859. His Official Report of the Niger Valley Exploring Party argues the case for emigration. Delany held that Black Americans must win a place of entire equality somewhere. He looked to the Niger valley as a land where a rising generation could rule itself.

The report describes the country, its peoples, its cotton, and its trade. It also answers critics of the emigration plan in strong terms. Delany's mission signed a treaty with Yoruba leaders for settlement land. The document stands as a founding text of Black nationalism, written before the Civil War freed the enslaved.
22239-security:
Security is a science fiction tale of a regimented future and a man saving for escape. Its Lancaster has two assets: his savings and an extra liquor ration. Tonight, coming home through the tube, he decides to make a dent in the whiskey. He ate at the commissary as usual but skipped the talk, thinking of the drink all the way home.

That small rebellion opens a story about control, rationing, and the price of safety. The future here runs on commissary meals, tubes, and allotted pleasures. Pulp writers used such sketches to test how much freedom men trade for security. The tale's chill comes from its quietness: nothing explodes, yet everything is owned.
22585-and-devious-the-line-of-duty:
And Devious the Line of Duty is a science fiction story of war and alliance among future worlds. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its politics turn on Jardeen, a large companion world whose space navy outmatches that of any other single world.

Neutral worlds wait to follow Jardeen's lead, so its choice of allies may decide a war. An alliance between Jardeen and the Verdam People's Worlds would, the narrator warns, quickly end the Terran Republic. The stakes are set out in the clipped style of pulp space opera. Readers who like grand strategy, rival star nations, and old magazine science fiction will find a compact example of the form.
22623-divinity:
Divinity is a science fiction story of a man adrift in space, weighing a desperate escape. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its hero, cut off from his ship and crew, thinks wildly for a moment before the risks of freedom in space come clear to him.

He must reach a civilized port, persuade the authorities he was shipwrecked and parted from his crew, then vanish into the crowd. The dangers are plain, but he takes them: anything beats running out of air and food alone in the dark. The story wrings tension from logistics and loneliness rather than monsters. It is a lean example of the stranded-spaceman tale from the magazine years.
2296-pillars-of-society:
Henrik Ibsen's Pillars of Society exposes a prosperous Norwegian town built on fraud and reputation. Consul Bernick, the town's leading citizen, has buried a scandal and a crime beneath his good works, and the return of old friends threatens to topple his pillars. Ibsen's four-act play builds its case like a prosecution.

The drama turns on Bernick's son, his sister-in-law, and the women who refuse to keep quiet any longer. Its ending, with a ship saved and a conscience faced, points toward Ibsen's later masterpieces. The play remains a sharp study of respectability and its costs.
23067-stories-of-animal-sagacity:
Cats and dogs open Stories of Animal Sagacity. The author begins with anecdotes of the sagacity shown by animals all readers know well. Anyone who watches a pet closely, the author says, will recognize the behavior. Readers will think of their own Tabby's tricks, or of a dog at home who once did nearly as clever a thing.

Anecdote follows anecdote, horses, elephants, birds, and more joining the cats and dogs. Each story argues that animals reason, remember, and feel more than people grant. Victorian natural history loved such collections, halfway between science and fireside wonder. The book's charm is its faith in close watching. It invites young readers to test every claim against the pet asleep by their own chair.
23290-the-dogs-dinner-party:
The Dog's Dinner Party is a story told through animals. One guest, a dog charged with watching over and protecting the livestock, fears he must decline his invitation. On second thoughts, he resolves to venture out anyway, since it is not a late dinner.

He can get away early, he reckons. His coat is rather the worse for wear, which troubles him. But he does own one handsome collar, at least. So he accepts. Readers get a genteel animal tale that plays human manners for gentle comedy: duty, dress, and dinner invitations, all weighed by a conscientious dog.
23478-self-denial-or-alice-wood-and-her-:
This moral tale for girls centres on Alice Wood and her missionary society, set around a village school on a pretty green ringed by old elms. Close by stands a candy shop kept by Mother Grimes, whose new cakes and candies tempt school children each day as they pass.

At recess, Alice runs among the schoolgirls whispering a plan: give up sweets, save the pennies, and send the money to missions far away. The tale follows the girls as they weigh treat against duty, and as small denials grow into a shared purpose. Young readers learn thrift, charity, and the strength of a group pledge, in a story that treats a child's pennies as a serious gift to a wider world.
23769-report-on-surgery-to-the-santa-cla:
J. Bradford Cox, M.D., read this report on surgery before the Santa Clara County Medical Society on March 2, 1880, and it was printed at San Jose the same year. Cox declines to repeat last year's history of surgery, and turns at once to first principles.

Surgery, he argues, is both a science and an art. Science is knowledge of nature and her laws; art is the application of that knowledge. From oxygen joining iron to form ferric oxide, he moves to the blood: about one-eighth of the body's weight, always in motion, made of plasma, red corpuscles, leucocytes, and granules. It is a clear statement of what a country doctor in 1880 thought his craft was.
2426-the-diary-of-a-man-of-fifty:
Henry James's Diary of a Man of Fifty follows a middle-aged traveler who revisits Florence and finds the woman he once loved, now older, and her daughter, who resembles her mother. The story turns on memory, regret, and the question of whether a second chance is a gift or a trap. James writes the Italian setting with his usual precision.

The tale's quiet tension comes from what the diarist will not quite admit to himself. It is a subtle study of aging and lost love. James readers will find a fine short work.
24735-stanford-stories-tales-of-a-young-:
Charles K. Field and Will H. Irwin wrote these Stanford stories, tales of a young university, published at New York in 1900 by Doubleday, Page. Their dedication greets Stanford as the newest sister university, still young, in Spanish dress of pillar, tile, and arch.

Field and Irwin, writing of a university still new, tell of students, cloisters, friendships, and the golden days of youth. Their stories scatter down four wide ways, but keep the power of those days. Readers will enjoy these warm, nostalgic tales of Stanford at the turn of the century.
24880-the-wreck-of-the-titan-or-futility:
Morgan Robertson published The Wreck of the Titan in 1898, in an edition that also holds The Pirates, Beyond the Spectrum, and In the Valley of the Shadow. The title tale pictures the Titan, the largest craft afloat, with bands, orchestras, doctors, chaplains, and a fire company for show. Her officers, picked from the Royal Navy, run her by hidden telegraph wires to every part of the ship.

Readers often note the tale's likeness to the later loss of the Titanic, though Robertson wrote fourteen years before that wreck. The other stories add jail-breakers, strange science, and dark valleys. The book remains famous for its eerie parallel and for its brisk, confident sea writing.
24928-longevity:
Therese Windser's science-fiction morality tale, in 1960 style, follows Captain Hinrik and the crew of the ship Semilunis to a sunken western continent. A scouting party pushes up a river into strange country, where exploration turns from mapping coastline to questioning what a long life is worth. The expedition's discoveries unsettle the crew's sense of purpose as much as their charts.

The strangest find is a cave with regular walls and a black surface divided into little squares, a relic that hints at an order older than the explorers. Windser uses the voyage to weigh longevity against meaning, asking whether extra years matter without a life worth living. The tale reads as a fable: a short, sharp story about ambition, time, and the price of both.
25006-psychology-and-social-sanity:
Hugo Münsterberg's 1914 volume, published by Doubleday, Page and dedicated to Dr. I. Adler, applies psychology to the social questions of its day. Chapters take up sex education, socialism, thought transference, and the mind of the juryman. Later chapters cover efficiency on the farm, social sins in advertising, the mind of the investor, society and the dance, and naïve psychology. Münsterberg writes as a public psychologist, translating laboratory ideas into civic advice.

The opening argues that the social question has shifted. Where it once meant the distribution of profit and wages, its predominant meaning is now the problem of sex, with its side issues of vice and social evil. A later chapter warns of the intellectual underworld. Its sham truths feed the longing for knowledge as vice feeds sensual desire, spreading germs more dangerous to national inner health than physical disease. The book is a period piece.
25201-the-lost-kitty:
Aunt Hattie's Lost Kitty, published in Boston in 1867, is a children's book built around a lost Maltese kitten. Fred Carleton finds the pretty cat and takes her in his arms, while his sister Hatty warns him that Ned Perry's family will grieve for her.

Chapters move from the kitten to Sabbath school, a drunkard, an ungrateful son, a strange visitor, and a grateful dog. Each short tale carries a moral, under the motto that thanks should be given in everything. The book is a gentle example of Victorian Sunday-school storytelling for young readers.
25388-the-herapath-property:
J. S. Fletcher's Herapath Property, published by Knopf in 1922, is a London mystery about a missing Member of Parliament. Jacob Herapath vanishes in the third week of his secretary Selwood's service, and the question Is It Murder opens the case.

Barthorpe takes charge, a pressman digs, and a taxi driver testifies. Clues pile up: a glass and a sandwich, a rosewood box, a diamond ring, a deserted flat, and a note in a prayer-book. A servant named Hancock noticed only an elbow chair pushed back and the electric light off. Fletcher weaves the net toward a second warrant.
25451-the-sleeping-beauty:
C. S. Evans retells the Sleeping Beauty tale, with pictures by Arthur Rackham. A king and queen, rich and beloved yet childless, long for a child of their own. At last a princess is born, and guests bring gifts: the king gives a white pony with red velvet saddle and gold bridle, while the queen gives a pearl necklace. Even the kitchen spit-boy carves a little wooden shoe, which the princess prizes as much as gold.

Only the queen is unhappy on the birthday, pale with worry over an old prophecy. She has carried the fear for fifteen years, and now the day has come. Heinemann published the London edition in 1920, with Lippincott in Philadelphia, in Rackham's rich picture-book style.
25457-manhood-of-humanity:
Alfred Korzybski argues for a new science and art he calls Human Engineering. He defines it as directing human energies and capacities toward human welfare. His key claim is that people differ from animals by using the work of the dead: each generation inherits past knowledge, tools, and power, and adds its own. He opens with a Brandeis warning that arithmetic is the first science and the mother of safety.

Korzybski counts three populations at work in the world: 1,600,000,000 living men, 10,000,000,000 living man-powers of the dead, and 1,600,000,000 sun man-powers. Sun-power, he says, equals the work of the whole living population. E. P. Dutton published the book in New York in 1921, with Korzybski writing from that city.
25868-the-young-railroaders-tales-of-adv:
F. Lovell Coombs gathers rail tales of young workers who solve hard problems with wire, wit, and nerve. Chapters take in one kind of wireless, a home made emergency battery, two tinkers who make good, an electrical detective, a race through flames, a secret telegram, and a runaway train. A haunted station, a ghost stepping grimly from its box, and a mind reading professor add color.

Printed by the Century Company in 1910, the book follows Jack and Alex through yards, shops, and small town shows, where a girls' club night and a church crowd test their plans. Each tale turns on a trick of the trade learned well and used at the right hour. The young railroaders win not by luck but by craft, pluck, and quick thought under strain.
25883-denslow-s-humpty-dumpty:
W. W. Denslow adapts and illustrates the old Humpty Dumpty rhyme as a picture tale for small children, printed in 1903. His Humpty is a cheerful, round fellow with a kind, generous spirit. One fear dogs him: his thin white skin may crack if he falls, and his heart wobbles as he walks, so he seeks the wise Black Hen for advice.

The hen recalls his father, old Humpty, who took warning from no one and paid for it on the wall. Denslow's hero fares better, and after a boil in the kettle he leaps out tough, bright, and spotted red like a circus clown. He frolics from table to chair, falls from shelves just to show how hard he is, and thanks the farmer's wife with fine manners.
26074-great-testimony-against-scientific:
Stephen Coleridge collects testimony against scientific cruelty in this 1918 volume from John Lane, first president of the National Anti Vivisection Society. Chapters honor Frances Power Cobbe, Cardinal Manning, Robert Browning, and other vice presidents, with eight pictures. The Earl of Shaftesbury opens the roll, a life spent for poor, weak, and lost. He freed women from hauling trucks underground on all fours and kept boys out of chimney climbs.

Later pages describe animal trials minute by minute, from violent abdominal efforts and convulsions in the first minute to stillness, dilated iris, and lost reflex in the second. Coleridge's book is a passionate brief that science without mercy wounds both beast and man, and that great voices across church, letters, and state condemned the practice.
26140-security:
Ernest M. Kenyon's short science-fiction story follows Collins, a researcher at a secret government laboratory at Fair Oaks, where passes, Geiger tests, and censored mail rule daily life. His work has lost its joy, his letters come back stamped as security violations, and even the journals he reads have grown thin and dull. Colleagues such as Gordon and Mason seem untroubled by rules that choke him.

The story tracks Collins's mounting strain as secrecy cuts him off from the open exchange that research needs to stay alive. Its title points to the price of that system: a mind kept under a lid, denied any outlet, will in the end find one of its own. Readers get a tense portrait of security culture and the human cost of working in silence.
26441-humanity-in-the-city:
The Reverend E. H. Chapin's 1854 discourses apply morality and religion to the daily life of a busy city. Chapin warns at the start that these themes do not exhaust preaching, and that an inward, holy life remains the spring of right feeling and clear sight. The city's problems, he hopes, will themselves convince readers of the need for that renewing principle.

Eight discourses follow: the lessons of the street, man and machinery, the strife for precedence, and the symbols of the republic. Then come the springs of social life, the allies of the tempter, the children of the poor, and the help of religion. Chapin praises citizens who hold liberty and law together, firm as steel and bright as gold, as the true greatness of a nation.
26534-the-girl-from-sunset-ranch-or-alon:
Amy Bell Marlowe's 1914 girls' novel sends Helen from Sunset Ranch eastward across the continent to a great city. Early chapters introduce Snuggy and the rose pony, Dudley Stone, and the mistress of Sunset Ranch, before the journey begins. At both ends of the route and across the continent, Helen travels toward a welcome that proves more tangled than she hoped.

In the city she searches out Sadie and her store, starting downtown after breakfast in Mr. Lawdor's little room and leaving by the area door as requested. She recalls the taxicab route uptown from her first evening, and the new sights crowd her attention. A ghost walk, a reputation to live up to, probing for facts, and time in the saddle carry Helen toward independence.
2703-the-argonauts-of-north-liberty:
Bret Harte opens this novel as the bell of North Liberty's Second Presbyterian Church stops ringing on a bleak Connecticut Sabbath. The town, never cheerful, looks bleaker still behind drawn curtains and half closed shutters, while the sun vainly coaxes a smile.

Harte's argonauts, eastern folk dreaming of California gold, carry their New England manners westward and collide with frontier life. The novel mixes satire of provincial piety with sympathy for restless dreamers. It offers a different Harte, turning his western lens back on the east that sent the gold seekers.
27052-sunny-boy-in-the-big-city:
Ramy Allison White's Sunny Boy in the Big City, published in 1920, takes its young hero from home to New York. The chapters follow a parade, a shopping trip, a ride on top of a bus, and a visit to Central Park, with Grant's Tomb and the Washington Square arch on the list.

Sunny Boy loses his room, gets lost, and is found again, helps the Harritys, and talks to the tall policeman directing traffic. Illustrated by Charles L. Wrenn, the book gives small readers a cheerful first tour of the city, full of sights, mishaps, and safe returns.
271-black-beauty:
Anna Sewell's Black Beauty tells a horse's life in his own voice, from a meadow colt to a London cab horse. Published in 1877, the novel follows Beauty through kind grooms and cruel masters, fires, accidents, and rest. Ginger, Merrylegs, and John Manly share his chapters.

Sewell, a Quaker invalid, wrote to plead for kinder treatment of horses: better bits, no bearing reins, and rest for tired animals. The book's plain moral force changed stable practice and law. Children still meet it as a first classic. Its plea for mercy outlived its century.
27212-the-life-of-the-party:
Irvin S. Cobb's The Life of the Party, published by Doran in 1919 with illustrations by James M. Preston, collects fiction, local color, and humor from the author of Back Home and Old Judge Priest. The frontispiece asks whether a man pays an election bet three weeks late or is simply a bedaddled idiot.

One story leaves its hero debating whether to enter a gathering in costume and deceive the company, or confess his predicament and seek a kindly soul's help. Footsteps from the dance hall drive him behind a pile of building material, in Cobb's warm comedy of embarrassment.
27213-the-heart-of-nature-or-the-quest-f:
Sir Francis Younghusband's The Heart of Nature, or The Quest for Natural Beauty, published by John Murray in 1921, seeks nature's beauty from the Sikkim Himalaya to Kashmir. The author, president of the Royal Geographical Society, opens with the sacred Ganges, the plains, and a first sight of the Himalaya.

Chapters follow the Teesta Valley's gorges and glens, the forest's butterflies, ferns, orchids, and rhododendrons, and Kinchinjunga at dawn and sunset. Younghusband argues that nature's activity is not mechanical but spiritual, with purposiveness, interdependence, and a common aspiration running through it.
27237-an-essay-on-the-scriptural-doctrin:
Reverend James Challis's An Essay on the Scriptural Doctrine of Immortality, published by Rivingtons in 1880, comes from the Plumian Professor of Astronomy at Cambridge. Challis notes a surprise: though disease, decay, and death abound, the words immortal and immortality occur in canonical Scripture only in the Epistles of Paul.

The words appear more often in the Apocrypha, in 2 Esdras, Wisdom of Solomon, and Ecclesiasticus, than in the canonical books. Challis argues that the Old Testament's apparent silence on so essential a doctrine finds its explanation in the course of his argument through the Gospel's light.
27601-hawtrey-s-deputy:
Harold Bindloss, author of The Impostor and The Liberationist, published this novel with Ward, Lock in London, Melbourne, and Toronto in 1910, illustrated by Cyrus Cuneo. Its chapters follow Sally Creighton, who takes charge, and Wyllard, who assents, through a crisis and the old country.

Agatha does not flinch, proves obdurate, and makes a decision, while fog, disillusion, and wanderers intervene. Later chapters bring the first ice, defeat, a delicate errand, a prior claim, and news of disaster. A rescue, the wilderness, and castaways follow, until Wyllard comes home. A frontispiece shows Wyllard's last doubt vanishing as he springs forward with a gasp. The novel is northern adventure and romance.
2773-fraternity:
John Galsworthy opens this novel on the last day of April, under a billowy sea of little broken clouds above High Street, Kensington. A patch of blue sky, shaped like a star, gleams like a single gentian flower among innumerable vapors.

Two sisters, a struggling writer, and a well meaning philanthropist tangle in questions of class, art, and brotherhood. Galsworthy writes with his quiet irony about London society and those it leaves out. The novel offers a study of fraternity as an ideal, and as a hard practice. Kensington's clouds mirror the characters' unsettled hopes.
27991-the-blue-bird-for-children-the-won:
Georgette Leblanc rendered her husband's play The Blue Bird into story form for children, edited and arranged for schools by Frederick Orville Perkins and translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos. The school edition, published by Silver, Burdett in 1914, is dedicated to the school children of America.

The wonderful adventures of Tyltyl and Mytyl in search of happiness follow the blue bird, an ancient symbol of happiness in Lorraine folklore. Leblanc's retelling brings Maeterlinck's delicate fantasy to young readers, and the teacher's note calls it one of the strongest imaginative works for children of its decade.
28208-the-gospel-day-or-the-light-of-chr:
Charles E. Orr wrote The Gospel Day, or The Light of Christianity, in 1904, published by the Gospel Trumpet Company at Moundsville, West Virginia. Orr divides Christian history into morning, noonday, and evening, tracing the church from light and Scripture through apostasy to a restored evening light. Chapters treat sin, salvation, the church, ordinances, divine healing, and the soul.

Orr says he claims no literary skill, only plain truth about a holy life, and thanks God for aid in the work. His tone is earnest and devotional, aimed at believers. The book offers a clear statement of Church of God teaching at the start of the twentieth century.
28312-atheism-in-pagan-antiquity:
A. B. Drachmann, professor of classical philology at Copenhagen, wrote Atheism in Pagan Antiquity, London and Copenhagen, 1922, as a study of unbelief in the ancient world. Drachmann shows that atheism and atheist, though formed from Greek roots, are not Greek words. Greeks said atheos and atheotes, close to ungodly and ungodliness, first as moral censure, later as a philosophical creed.

Philosophers bore atheos as a surname, and the word covered both denial of gods in theory and practical denial, as Jews and Christians denied the gods of state. Drachmann writes with scholarly care. The book offers a clear, learned guide to ancient atheism.
28459-in-brief-authority:
F. Anstey's In Brief Authority, published in London in 1915, was planned and mostly written before the First World War, as Anstey notes with sadness. He left its German characters and incidents unaltered, unwilling to believe that nursery friends of youth could ever be regarded as enemies.

The story opens in March at Inglegarth, Gablehurst, where Mrs. Sidney Wibberley-Stimpson, newly enriched by a legacy, sits alone in her drawing-room awaiting a caller. Chapters with titles such as Crowned Heads, Cares of State, and Servants of the Queen suggest a comic fantasy of ordinary people raised to sudden authority. Anstey writes the social comedy for which he was known.
28805-dorothy-s-house-party:
Evelyn Raymond wrote this 1908 girls' story about Dorothy and the house party she gathers. The book opens at the end of a country fair. It moves through choosing guests and the arrival of an uninvited one, and follows riddles, morning calls, churchgoing, music, and a supposed apparition by the lily pond. Later chapters bring a marvelous tale, the finding of money, and the story of the worm that turned.

Dorothy's party mixes everyday social comedy with small mysteries that resolve kindly. Raymond writes for young readers who enjoy conversation, friendship, and a touch of the uncanny without real fright. The book gives a pleasant picture of American country-house life for girls in the early 1900s, told in a warm and easy style.
28998-social-life-or-the-manners-and-cus:
Maud C. Cooke wrote this 1896 guide to the manners and customs of polite society, published in Buffalo by Matthews-Northrup. The book gives rules of etiquette for all occasions, forming a complete guide to self-culture in conversation, dress, deportment, correspondence, and the care of children and the home. Colored phototypes illustrate it, and the preface quotes the saying that manners make the man.

The first department treats introductions and salutations, with rules constantly observed in good society. Later departments cover the table, calls, weddings, and mourning, though the sample shows only the opening. Readers get a full Victorian etiquette book, useful both as social history and as a window into how Americans of 1896 wanted to appear at their best.
29408-wanderer-of-infinity:
Harl Vincent published this story in Astounding Stories in March 1933. Bert Redmond, who never heard of Lenville until Joan's letter arrived, finds it a tiny village among the Ramapo hills of lower New York State, a few miles from Tuxedo. A prim white church, a general store with a gasoline pump, and a dozen weatherbeaten frame houses make up the place.

Bert stops his battered flivver at a corner where a group of onlookers gathers, in a dusty crossroads hamlet thirty years out of date. In unmapped realms of infra-dimensional space, the magazine says, Bert meets a pathetic figure, the Wanderer. Readers get a pulp tale where a quiet village road opens onto infinity, and a wanderer carries its sorrow.
29733-the-farmer-and-his-community:
Dwight Sanderson, professor of rural social organization at Cornell University, published this study in New York in 1922. His editor's preface looks back to early New England towns, true communities with their own church, school, and town meeting. The westward tide then made the farm family the unit of rural life, with neighborhoods, local schools, and a crowd of churches taking the place of one town.

Sanderson treats the farm home, markets, cooperation, education, religious life, health, play, and government in turn. He closes with community organization, planning, and loyalty. The book argues that farmers need a strong local group larger than the neighborhood, as the Grange had shown. It is a clear, practical work on how country folk can live and act together.
29962-celebrity:
James McKimmey, Jr., wrote Celebrity, with pictures by Paul Orban. Its opening date is June 19, 1978, Celebrity Day. The city stretches awake: empty streets glisten from a water truck's bath, dew-wet grass winks in fresh sun, and a boy on a bicycle throws tightly rolled newspapers down an elm-bordered avenue. Lights snap on in a thousand windows against the cool whiteness of dawn.

Men blink at beard-stubbled chins, women move sleepily toward porcelain and chrome kitchens, and a truck roars as garbage pails rattle. Sour orange rinds, wet leaves, unfolding flowers, toasting bread, and frying bacon fill the air. Transcribed music and commercial announcers blare, then doors shut and sounds mute. A million people shift, stretch, and scratch as the sun rises on Celebrity Day.
30065-benign-stupors-a-study-of-a-new-ma:
August Hoch wrote Benign Stupors, a study of a new manic-depressive reaction type, printed in New York in 1921 by the Macmillan Company. Hoch had been director of the Psychiatric Institute of the New York State Hospitals on Ward's Island and professor of psychiatry at Cornell University Medical College. He dedicates the book to his former colleagues in the New York State hospital service. An editor's preface tells the book's origin and history.

Hoch, on becoming director in 1910, discovered an interest already present in exactly the kind of psychiatric research he hoped to advance. His predecessor Adolf Meyer had taught that psychoses should be seen as psychobiological reactions, not rigid nosological entities, and had demanded scrupulously thorough records of what each patient said and did. Fifteen chapters follow, from typical cases of deep stupor and partial stupor reactions through suicidal cases, affect, catalepsy, diagnosis, treatment, and a summary.
30194-landmarks-in-the-history-of-early-:
Kirsopp Lake, Winn Professor of Ecclesiastical History at Harvard, traces early Christianity as a series of syntheses across five landmarks. Galilee opens with the Jewish world, the Kingdom of God, and the teaching of Jesus beside his Jewish contemporaries. Jerusalem follows with the synoptic problem, Acts, communism, and messianic doctrine, while Antioch tracks the spread of the faith and Paul's visits.

Macmillan published the London volume in 1920. Later chapters treat Corinth as a Graeco-Oriental cult, then Rome and Ephesus, with Paul, adoptionism, the Fourth Gospel, the doctrine of the Logos, Justin Martyr, and Origen. Lake writes as a scholar for educated readers, weighing sources and ideas rather than telling saints' lives. The book stands as a compact, critical map of the first Christian centuries.
30392-twelve-causes-of-dishonesty:
Rev. Henry Ward Beecher gives Twelve Causes of Dishonesty in Altemus' Eternal Life Series. Selections from religious authors, printed and bound in leatherette with designs in silver and ink, cost twenty-five cents per volume. Companion volumes include Eternal Life by Henry Drummond, Lord, Teach Us to Pray by Andrew Murray, and God's Word and God's Work by Martin Luther. Faith by Thomas Arnold and The Creation Story by William E. Gladstone follow.

Beecher opens with a survey of panic and ruin, when sober men expected oriental tales. Then sudden frosts, storms, and blight swept harvests away in a day, firms rent like oak by lightning, and merchants ruined by thousands. Banks exploded, robbed, or fleeced by astounding forgeries. Out of that reverse swarmed dishonest men. Beecher turns to an enumeration of causes, beginning with men who find in their bosom from the first an inclination to dishonest ways.
30610-history-of-human-society:
Frank W. Blackmar, professor of sociology at the University of Kansas, writes History of Human Society, copyrighted in 1926 by Charles Scribner's Sons. Part one, Civilization and Progress, opens by asking what civilization is, noting the human trail and material signs everywhere.

Early humans faced an unknown world, Blackmar writes, and civilization expresses itself in many ways, with progress as an essential trait. Modern civilization rests on fundamentals, diversity aids progress, and the goal of civilized man remains an open question. Blackmar offers a textbook survey of society, progress, and human development for students and general readers.
30722-subjectivity:
Norman Spinrad writes Subjectivity, a science fiction story from Analog, January 1964, illustrated by Leo Summers, opening with boredom on a long interstellar trip as quite a problem. The government's entertainment technique for this trip, Spinrad hints, was a little too good.

By the story's start, travel between planets is routine, and people have settled the worlds and moons of the Sun's system. Attention then shifts outward, only to stall: thirty years of effort leave researchers sure that no drive faster than light can work within any theory they know. The researchers quit, yet a single world government, which now rules all human homes, refuses to quit with them. Spinrad turns boredom, government, and star travel into a wry tale.
30759-exit-betty:
Grace Livingston Hill wrote this novel about a young bride named Betty, full name Elizabeth Stanhope, who faints at her own wedding. On a wet November night Betty rides to church in bridal finery, small and frightened, with a florid cousin, almost unknown until hours before, to give her away. The gray-haired cousin of her own mother, who had long promised to give her away, sent word only an hour before that he was unavoidably detained.

At the altar, before a tall, dark, frowning bridegroom and a church full of guests, Betty sinks in a heap as the minister begins. Her stepmother scolds her in the vestry for making a spectacle. Hill builds the tale from that fraught opening: a girl pressed toward a marriage she dreads, by people who claim to care for her welfare. It is a sentimental romance with a strong, sympathetic heroine.
30940-peggy-owen-and-liberty:
Lucy Foster Madison, author of Peggy Owen, Peggy Owen, Patriot, and Peggy Owen at Yorktown, wrote this story. It was published by the Penn Publishing Company in 1913, with copyright in 1912 and pictures by H. J. Peck. Its verse gives the motto: liberty throughout the land, and good to all their brother race. Freedom's scroll was sealed where the dawn of reason broke on the trampled rights of man.

Twenty chapters run from A Small Dinner Becomes a Party and Peggy Is Surprised through On the Horns of a Dilemma, The Search, Friends in Need, and Appearances Against Her. They continue with David Owen Is Informed of the Facts, Before the Council, Out of the Frying-Pan into the Fire, and A Race for Life. They continue with The Choice of Fairfax, They Must Go Home, A Woman's Wit, and Marching Orders. They end with The Attack on the Blockhouse.
3118-equality:
Charles Dudley Warner opens this short essay with a blunt counterclaim: all men are created unequal. Writing in the late nineteenth century, he takes up equality as most people used the word after the middle of the eighteenth century, a vague popular slogan rather than a precise idea. He warns that the slogan is often mixed up with uniformity, as if making people equal meant making them alike.

Warner tests the doctrine against nature, which works by equal laws yet yields endless diversity, and against old revolts that fought hardship more than they argued theory. His point is that a just sense of equality must leave room for unlikeness. The essay still serves as a sharp check on loose talk about sameness, fairness, and what a free society can rightly promise.
31193-manifesto-of-the-communist-party:
Karl Marx and Frederick Engels's Manifesto of the Communist Party, in the authorized English translation edited and annotated by Engels, appeared in 1908. The Labor News Company published it in New York at ten cents. It opens with its famous warning that a specter is haunting Europe, the specter of Communism. All the powers of old Europe, it says, from Pope and Czar to Metternich and Guizot, have joined to exorcise it.

The first chapter declares the history of all hitherto existing society to be the history of class struggles, from freeman and slave through lord and serf to guildmaster and journeyman. It calls on Communists to publish their views openly. Short, fierce, and world-changing, the Manifesto remains the founding text of modern communism.
31626-the-vilbar-party:
Evelyn E. Smith's science-fiction story The Vilbar Party, illustrated by Kossin and produced from Galaxy Science Fiction of January 1955, opens with Professor Slood cajoling Narli Gzann about a party. Slood says the Perzils host a vilbar party the next night, and Narli will come this time, will he not. Narli, rubbing his forehead fretfully and nibbling a frismil nut from the tray on his desk, reminds Slood how he feels about parties.

The party is in Narli's honor, a farewell, since he is leaving to take another teaching job. Slood insists it would be unthinkable for Narli to stay away, though he cannot answer for his friend's unsociable conduct. Smith's story, as its sidenote jokes, turns on what Earthmen would tell Narli, only with frismil nuts. Readers will find a light, alien comedy of manners.
31659-side-stepping-with-shorty:
Sewell Ford's Side-stepping with Shorty was published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York with copyright in 1908 by Mitchell Kennerley and illustrations by Francis Vaux Wilson. Its contents list Shorty and the Plute, rounding up Maggie, up against Bentley, the Tortonis' star act, and putting Pinckney on the job. They continue with the soaring of the Sagawas, Rinkey and the phony lamp, Pinckney and the twins, and a line on Peacock Alley. A frontispiece caption boasts that they tackle anything Shorty leads them up to.

Ford writes in the vernacular humor of his day, with Shorty as a small-time fixer who sidesteps trouble by wit. Each chapter is a fresh scheme, with a new set of characters to manage. Readers of American humorous fiction will find a lively, slangy collection, where Shorty's sidestep is always quicker than the trouble chasing him.
31822-atlanta-a-twentieth-century-city:
Issued by the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce in 1904, this pamphlet presents Atlanta as a twentieth-century city, with a cover reproducing the Harper's Weekly picture Atlanta by Night of October 10, 1903. It tells how Atlanta grew, twice built on the same site for its natural advantages.

By the eve of the Civil War, Atlanta counted 11,000 residents and hummed with trade. It was a depot for supplies and a seat of industries sustaining Confederate military operations, before its destruction and rebuilding. Readers get a booster pamphlet of the New South, proud of growth, railroads, and commerce, and illustrated with views of the rebuilt city.
31964-brknk-s-bounty:
Jerry Sohl's short story Brknk's Bounty was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in January 1955. It is narrated by a former newspaper man who has spent a year in circus life and never wants to give it up. He works all summer and gets the winter off. It is a better job than any he could get in the newspaper racket, where he might have been city editor or merely a rewrite man.

The narrator thanks, grudgingly, Trlk the Sybillian, whom he first saw on a July morning at the start of the vacation schedule, for all the trouble that led him to the circus. Readers get a comic science-fiction tale in which a feature writer becomes the feature attraction, in a booze-to-riches success story.
31997-miss-muffet-s-christmas-party:
Samuel McChord Crothers's Christmas fantasy, published in November 1902 with drawings by Olive M. Long, gives the nursery-rhyme heroine a party of her own. Miss Muffet and the spider, now on friendly terms, decide against inviting flies and settle instead on a literary party, inviting every person Miss Muffet has read about. Together they write the invitations on cobweb paper, some informal and some in full formal style.

The guest list runs through the books of childhood. It includes Little Bo-Peep and Red Riding-Hood, the Swiss Robinson family, and visitors from Wonderland and Lilliput.
