Tom Sawyer, Alice, and Aladdin feature in its illustrations. The fun lies in practical problems. One is finding the right address for a traveller between Norwich and the Moon. Another is wording invitations for kings known only as a certain king.
32006-modern-substitutes-for-christianit:
Pearson McAdam Muir, minister of Glasgow Cathedral and chaplain in ordinary to the King, wrote this defence of Christianity against its modern rivals. It was first published in December 1909, with a second edition in October 1912. Muir opens with popular charges against the faith: that it belongs to rude, unenlightened ages, that modern science has outgrown it, and that Jesus has had his day. He answers those charges across six chapters.

Each chapter takes up one substitute in turn. They cover morality without religion, the religion of the universe, the religion of humanity, and theism without Christ. A final chapter gathers the tribute that critics themselves have paid to Christ. Appendices and a list of authorities consulted close the book. Readers get a plain, argumentative survey of Edwardian religious debate from a convinced churchman's side.
32032-second-variety:
Philip K. Dick's short story, printed in Space Science Fiction in May 1953, is set in a ruined war zone where machines do the killing. Its tagline warns that the claws were bad enough at first: nasty, crawling little death-robots. Once the machines started copying people, peace became the only hope left for humanity, and even that looked doubtful. The opening follows a Russian soldier climbing a ragged hillside, gun ready, through ash and debris.

Eric and Corporal Leone track the soldier through a view sight, debating whether to fire. Leone holds them back, judging that they are not needed. The tension comes from a simple question: in a war of imitation machines, who can be trusted as human? Readers get a bleak story about weapons that learn to wear their makers' faces, and soldiers who must decide what counts as a person.
32040-diplomatic-immunity:
Robert Sheckley's short story Diplomatic Immunity was printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in August 1953 and illustrated by Ashman. It opens with a tagline: its hero said he was not immortal, but nothing could kill him, yet if Earth was to live as a free world, he had to die. Colonel Cercy accepts a chair in the very special suite the State Department has given the Ambassador. He tries to size up the individual who has all Washington chewing its fingernails.

The Ambassador hardly looks like a menace: medium height, slight build, in a conservative brown tweed suit the State Department gave him, with an intelligent, finely molded, aloof face. Readers get a Cold War science-fiction tale of an alien envoy, a scientist's reports, and a question with no clean answer.
32098-the-pentecost-of-calamity:
Owen Wister, author of The Virginian, published this book with Macmillan in August 1915, and it was reprinted through that autumn. Its title comes from an Emerson epigraph about a fiery Pentecost girding a countless host with one flame. Wister writes as an American looking back at a Europe sliding into war, and at a Germany he had loved, now changed by conflict.

His reflections turn on memory and contrast. He recalls a peaceful scene in the heart of Germany on a June day in 1914, and sets it against the war that followed. He quotes a German in Brussels who said Belgium must suffer, even disappear, rather than see the German Empire torpedoed by treacherous enemies. Wister argues that Germany had long crouched for its spring, and that the war it incubated repeated the old dream of world conquest. Readers get a wartime American meditation.
321-moran-of-the-lady-letty:
Frank Norris promises a story of a battle, at least one murder, and several sudden deaths. Moran of the Lady Letty opens, oddly, at a pink tea for debutante Josie Herrick in San Francisco. Ross Wilbur arrives too early and faces a terrifying array of millinery.

Wilbur is soon shanghaied aboard the Lady Letty, where Captain Moran rules a brutal crew. The pink-tea world gives way to forecastles, storms, and murder. Norris dedicated the book to a life-saving captain. The novel mixes society comedy with sea adventure. Norris's sea tale followed his California novels of greed and fate.
32307-a-brief-account-of-radio-activity:
Francis P. Venable's A Brief Account of Radio-Activity was published by D. C. Heath and Company in Boston, New York, and Chicago in 1917. It is a popular account of the science. Venable, professor of chemistry at the University of North Carolina and author of A Short History of Chemistry and Periodic Law, writes for readers who want the facts without mathematics. His first chapter treats the discovery of radio-activity.

That chapter covers the beginning, radio-active bodies, an atomic property, and new bodies, including polonium and radium. A second chapter treats the properties of radiations. It covers ionization of gases, photographing the track of a ray, action on photographic plates, and scintillations on phosphorescent bodies. It continues through penetrating power, magnetic deflection, and the three types of rays, alpha, beta, and gamma. Readers get a 1917 primer on radioactivity, written while the science was still new.
32351-voyage-to-eternity:
Milton Lesser's story, printed in Imagination in July 1953, opens in a city bracing for another round of riots. The cover line says Temple, if drafted, faced parting from Earth and his loved girl, yet hardest was knowing return was barred. When May sunlight covers the tree-lined avenues of Center City, rioting starts.

People gather in angry knots outside city hall, meet in the park and litter its walks with papers as they gobble editorial comment. They slip through back alleys at night to plan with furious futility. Center City's finest know when to make themselves scarce, since their uniforms stand for everything objectionable at this time. Center City, like most towns in United North America, has lived through the Riots before and will live through them again. Readers get a future America of riots, drafts, and a one-way voyage.
32408-marie-antoinette-and-the-downfall-:
Imbert de Saint-Amand's history, translated by Elizabeth Gilbert Martin and published in New York in 1899 with a portrait, follows Marie Antoinette through the downfall of French royalty. Contents open with Paris at the beginning of 1792, Count de Fersen's last journey to Paris, and the deaths of Emperor Leopold and Gustavus III. Madame Roland enters the scene, first as a rising figure, then as minister of the interior's wife, alongside Dumouriez as foreign minister.

Later chapters cover the declaration of war, the disbanding of the constitutional guard, the sufferings of Louis XVI, Roland's dismissal, and a three days' ministry. The narrative builds toward June twentieth and the invasion of the Tuileries, with Marie Antoinette at its centre. Saint-Amand writes a vivid, sympathetic account of revolution's closing months for the monarchy.
32451-women-of-early-christianity:
Alfred Brittain and Mitchell Carroll's study, volume three of Woman in All Ages and in All Countries, examines women of early Christianity, with an introduction by J. Cullen Ayer junior of Harvard. Published in Philadelphia in 1907, it opens with women of the Western Empire and the women of the gospel narrative. An opening plate, Seeking Shelter after Luc Olivier Merson, reflects on Mary of Nazareth as Virgin, Mother, and Saint.

The authors argue that Mary's halo owes its glow to her Son's moral splendour. Her place at the head of all daughters of earth rests on an ideal gathered from grace, beauty, and purity. Later parts follow Christian women through the early church, martyrdom, and monastic life. The book gives readers a broad, illustrated survey of women's place in the first Christian centuries.
32705-deadly-city:
Ivar Jorgenson tells of a man who wakes in darkness, drugged and struck on the head. He finds himself sealed inside a cement chamber. Crawling through dust and cobwebs, he finds a wooden trap in the ceiling. He climbs into a sunlit alley, where no one is in sight and the city stands empty.

He joins other survivors, among them Frank, Nora, and Jim Wilson. They hear a strange howling that seems to come from many places at once. Unseen invaders circle the doomed city. Yet the greater danger proves to be the survivors themselves, who turn guns on one another while the alien presence closes in.
32739-probability:
Louis Trimble tells a bartender's strange tale, in this story from If Worlds of Science Fiction of April 1954, illustrated by Ed Emsh. Mike Murphy narrates. For thirty-one years a scared little man has slipped into his saloon at five-ten each weekday evening for one glass of beer.

The man is Rabelais Pettis, a draftsman for Cartner and Dillson, at the same desk from 1922 to 1953. His hobby is inventing, though he says he cannot get raw materials. One day he offers Murphy the saloon itself, fur coats, dolls, and a run for Congress. Then, at five-nine, Pettis walks in again and roars for two beers, and Murphy wonders whether he dreamed it all before.
32847-the-door-into-infinity:
Edmond Hamilton tells of the Brotherhood of the Door, in this story from Weird Tales of August and September 1936. Paul Ennis, a tall young American, married Ruth in New York only last week. On their second day in London he sees her swept into a limousine and driven off before his eyes.

Inspector Pierce Campbell of Scotland Yard repeats a strange catechism to him. The Door leads outside the world. Those Beyond the Door taught his forefathers to open it, and sacrifices are brought to them. Campbell is certain the Brotherhood kidnapped Ruth. A cutter fight, an escape by motor-boat, and a hooded rite in a cavern follow, as Ennis takes the place of the priest Chandra Dass to reach his wife.
33096-years-of-plenty:
Ivor Brown's Years of Plenty, first published in London in 1915, follows Martin Leigh from school to university in two books. Book one opens with Martin gazing at the wooden walls of his cubicle after his first day as a boarder at a public school. He is overwhelmed by all there is to remember. The list runs from his form and form master and his desks to his place in chapel and at meals, his hours of work and his field for play.

Book two carries Martin to university, where youth's wealth is spent well and decently, as the Hilaire Belloc epigraph puts it, though whether it is lost no one can tell. Brown writes a coming-of-age novel fond of school and university life. It remains a warm, reflective story of growing up in England just before the First World War changed that world for good.
33117-thirty:
Howard Vincent O'Brien's Thirty is a novel of a man at the age of its title, facing the choices that youth postpones. It was published in New York in 1915 and illustrated by Robert W. Amick. Its chapters run from an uninvited guest through oil and water to burned bridges and a bluff called.

O'Brien, author of New Men for Old, dedicates the book to his mother. She sought always to make him love the truth, though knowing his truth would not, in the nature of things, be hers. That dedication sets the novel's theme: a son's truth against a mother's, and a young man's search for his own code at thirty. The novel remains a thoughtful period story of coming of age, written with candor and a keen eye for social life.
33237-the-call-of-the-world-or-every-man:
W. E. Doughty's book calls every man to the supreme opportunity of world missions, in a revised edition published in 1913. As educational secretary of the Laymen's Missionary Movement, Doughty argues that world conditions now favor the spread of Christianity. The world is accessible, plastic, and changing, and Christians must answer with widening vision. His chapters map that call in plain, urgent prose.

The book is both a survey and a summons, aimed at laymen who might give, go, or pray for missions. Its tone is earnest and hopeful, rooted in the missionary enthusiasm of its age. For readers of church history, it captures a moment when many believed the whole world lay open to the gospel, and that the time to act was now.
33444-sulamith-a-romance-of-antiquity:
Alexandre Kuprin's Sulamith, a romance of antiquity translated from the Russian by B. G. Guerney, was privately printed for subscribers. The year was 1928. Its fifteen hundred numbered copies tell a tale of ancient love. Eight full-page color illustrations by Forbes-Felix grace a book printed on fine laid paper with type distributed after printing. Kuprin, author of Yama, writes of a world long past with rich, sensual prose.

The romance's appeal lies in its exotic, biblical-age setting and its tender, tragic love story. Its tone is lush and poetic, suited to readers who love historical romance of the old school. For fans of Kuprin, Sulamith offers a beautiful, limited-edition tale of a queen and a king, love and fate.
33567-janet-hardy-in-radio-city:
Ruthe S. Wheeler follows young film actress Janet Hardy from a studio location shoot to New York. Janet wins a leading part, works through fire scenes and a studio blaze with her friend Helen Thorne. Janet travels east, where Radio City and its rehearsal rooms open a larger stage. Along the way she tries her hand at writing, wears costumes fitted for the camera, and learns how a production is put together.

A vanished manuscript turns the second half of the thirty-chapter story into a mystery. Janet faces insinuations, a shadowed hallway, and a night on the twenty-seventh floor before she finds a clue. The novel mixes backstage detail with detective suspense, aimed at readers who enjoy stories of girls making their way in show business.
33643-in-the-day-of-adversity:
A French historical romance signed J. B. -B., inspired by the secret memoirs of the Comte de Bussy Rabutin and Rousset's history of Louvois, follows Georges St. Georges. He faces danger in the reign of Louis XIV. The story opens in snow across Franche-Comté. The story moves through a king's command, hospitality, a marquise's tale, a minister of war, a galley called the Grande Réale, and a chapter dated May 1692.

Thirty-five chapters plus a conclusion carry St. Georges toward La Hogue, escapes, snares, a day of execution, and a final reckoning. The novel blends court intrigue, military adventure, and romance, with a hero caught between royal power and private enemies. Readers of swashbuckling historical fiction will enjoy its pace, its period color, and its old-fashioned sense of honor under adversity.
33701-fraternal-charity:
The Reverend Father Valuy, a Jesuit already favorably known to English readers through several translations, offers a short treatise on fraternal charity, taken from his larger work on the religious life. The authorized translation, published by Benziger Brothers in 1908, notes that charity is so important a factor in community life that the little book should supply a want felt by many. Though written specially for religious, it aims to benefit seculars in every sphere of life.

Chapters treat charity as the peculiar virtue of Christ, fundamental truths, the family spirit, egotism or self-seeking, and twelve characteristics of fraternal charity, followed by preservatives against its loss. Valuy writes plainly about love as the sunshine of existence, wanted everywhere. The treatise suits readers seeking a practical, traditional guide to living charitably in community.
33741-the-acquisitive-society:
R. H. Tawney, fellow of Balliol College, Oxford, and late member of the Coal Industry Commission, examines the acquisitive society in this 1920 Harcourt, Brace volume. Eleven chapters move from an introduction through rights and functions, the acquisitive society itself, the nemesis of industrialism, property and creative work, the functional society, industry as a profession, the vicious circle.

Tawney opens by noting that Englishmen combine sustained practical energy with reluctance to test their activity against principles. They care more for the state of the roads than for their place on the map. He argues that industry should serve function rather than acquisition. The book remains a classic of Christian socialist thought and a sharp critique of profit as the organizing aim of economic life.
356-beyond-the-city:
Arthur Conan Doyle sets this gentle novel in a row of new villas on the edge of London. Two elderly sisters watch their neighbors with keen, kind curiosity, and the arrival of new folk at number three stirs talk. Soon a retired admiral, a doctor, and a young couple fill the street with fresh life.

Gossip, courtship, and small town manners drive the plot, with a darker note when past deeds catch up with one resident. Doyle writes with warmth and humor, far from his detective tales. The book charms as a portrait of late Victorian suburb life, where news travels fast over garden fences.
3614-an-exhortation-to-peace-and-unity:
This Puritan treatise on Christian unity is printed among the works of John Bunyan, though its authorship has been questioned. An editor's note explains that the piece appears in nearly all collected editions of Bunyan, yet the Reverend Mr Philip, in his Life and Times of Bunyan, doubted that Bunyan wrote it. The present edition appends it separately, without settling the question.

The treatise expounds the call to keep the unity of the Spirit, arguing that God's Spirit cannot be divided, so believers must labor to stay at peace with one another. It suits readers interested in Puritan preaching and in the problem of division among Christians. Those who want Bunyan beyond doubt should turn to his signed works.
3751-the-psychology-of-beauty:
Ethel Puffer wrote this study to ask a plain question with scientific care, namely why some forms please the eye and others do not. She reviews the theories of her day, from German writers on perception to English critics of art, and tests them against the experience of looking. The pleasure of form, she argues, lies in a fresh, lively, and yet effortless activity of the organs that take in shape, color, and line.

Later chapters weigh repose against energy, unity against variety, and the eye's share against the whole body's response. Puffer writes for educated readers rather than specialists, and her examples stay close to pictures, buildings, and common sights. The book now reads as an early landmark in the psychology of art, careful, earnest, and refreshingly free of jargon.
4237-australian-search-party:
Charles Henry Eden wrote this account for Illustrated Travels, the geography journal edited by H. W. Bates, after a cyclone struck the Queensland coast in the autumn of 1866. The storm wrecked settlements at Cardwell and Townsville and lost the small schooner Eva, sailing from Cleveland toward Rockingham Bay with goods and people aboard.

When reports reached Cardwell that white men had been seen among the tribes near the Herbert River, local men formed a search party to rescue any survivors or learn their fate. Eden describes the river country, the search itself, and the fear of captivity among peoples little known to settlers, giving a settler's-eye view of frontier Queensland.
4293-neal-the-miller-a-son-of-liberty:
James Otis wrote this boys' story of the American Revolution around Neal, a young miller in New Hampshire. Neal lacks two years of his majority, but his late father gave him his time before Governor Wentworth himself. With help from his friend Andrew McCleary, Neal plans to build a grist-mill and find its machinery.

The chapters follow the project, an escape, and a trip to Boston. They follow work on the Pascataqua, and the characters Stephen Kidder and Sewatis. Otis mixes adventure with the politics of the colonies. Neal learns to watch the law on arms, and to weigh loyalty to friends against loyalty to the colonial cause.
4509-three-acres-and-liberty:
Bolton Hall wrote this book on small farming and freedom, in a revised edition published by Macmillan in 1918, after its first appearance in 1907. His foreword argues that people are not truly tied to desk or bench, but only think they are tied. He recalls a horse in Montana, hobbled nightly to keep it from wandering.

Hall's theme is that three acres, worked with sense, can give a family food, health, and independence from wages. The book belongs to the back-to-the-land movement, practical about soil, crops, and markets. Readers today will find its argument for smallholding and self-reliance still lively, if dated in detail.
4556-a-woman-of-thirty:
Marjorie Allen Seiffert published this book of poems in New York in 1919, arranging her work in five parts. The first part, The Old Woman, is a morality play in verse. Later parts gather love poems for summer and autumn, studies and designs, and an interlude of mountain trails and family poems. An elegy sequence closes the book. Titles range from Singalese love songs and a temple sequence to portraits, a police station scene, and a desert picnic.

Seiffert moves freely between far places and home life, between a Japanese vase, an Italian chest, and a child, a father, or an absent friend. Her poems are short, image-led, and often wistful, with a modern freedom of form. Readers get a varied early twentieth-century poetry book, where love, loss, and travel sit beside quiet domestic scenes, and where a woman's thirtieth year becomes a lens for looking back and forward.
4710-the-story-of-electricity:
John Munro, author of Electricity and Its Uses and Pioneers of Electricity, wrote The Story of Electricity for the general reader. His preface says electricity needs little recommendation, since it shapes daily comfort, industry, and civilisation itself. Anyone who imagines all electrical service suddenly ceasing, he argues, will grasp its claims to attentive study.

Munro aims to present the essential facts of electrical science in a popular form, showing principles and the means by which they serve mankind. The book suits readers with no technical training who want to understand lights, wires, motors, and telegraphs. Readers get a clear, early popular science book, written before radio and modern electronics, and a useful window into how electricity first entered ordinary life.
5882-a-district-messenger-boy-and-a-neck:
A District Messenger Boy and a Necktie Party opens with unwilling passengers and a boy named Joe Curtis, number two hundred and ninety-seven. Asked his name and number, Joe listens to exact orders. A man goes to Providence by Sound steamer sailing in an hour and a half. Joe must take tickets, go to the boat's office, and get a key. From that errand, a dime-novel adventure of messages, danger, and a necktie party unfolds.

Readers get fast, plain melodrama in the messenger-boy tradition, where a working boy's reliability is tested by criminals and chance. The story favors action and clear villains over fine psychology. It suits readers curious about late nineteenth-century popular fiction, and fans of boy heroes whose honesty carries them through rough company.
5949-beasley-s-christmas-party:
Booth Tarkington's Beasley's Christmas Party, illustrated by Ruth Sypherd Clements and dedicated to James Whitcomb Riley in October 1909, opens on a maple-bordered street as still as a country Sunday. A narrator talks with a woman about Mr Beasley's house beyond a fence, and about Mr Dowden, who cut the narrator off pointedly when the old place was mentioned. The woman muses, eyes falling then rising, her far-away gaze resting on the house.

Here is a Christmas story of memory, embarrassment, and old houses holding old feelings. Tarkington favors quiet conversation and atmosphere over plot machinery, letting a party become an occasion for reckoning. The book suits readers who enjoy holiday stories with a reflective turn, and fans of Tarkington's Indiana tales of youth, age, and home.
6753-psmith-in-the-city:
P. G. Wodehouse sends Psmith and Mike into the city, to business careers neither quite wants. The contents list Mr. Bickersdyke walking behind the bowler's arm, Mike hearing bad news, a new era, first steps in business, and Psmith explaining things in his own grand way. A haunting, a cheque, and stirring times on the common follow.

Psmith's talk, Mike's cricket, and Bickersdyke's bluster make a comic trio, with the city as a new kind of school. Wodehouse keeps the farce light and the dialogue bright. Psmith in the City is a gay, early Wodehouse novel of youth, work, and friendship.
6955-the-prince-and-betty:
Wodehouse opens The Prince and Betty with a cable from Mervo, a small kingdom whose prince and politics drive the comedy. A pretty girl in a blue dress crosses a terrace to Elsa Keith and Marvin Rossiter beneath a great sycamore, where an engagement already binds the pair. Later chapters bring John, Mister Scobell and his shifting schemes, an ultimatum from the throne, and a change in Mervo's constitution.

Betty makes a friend, policy changes, and a newspaper office called Peaceful Moments becomes a battleground of staff, cats, and campaigns. The tale runs through visits, battles, and a final attempt before its conclusion. Wodehouse keeps the tone light, with a prince, a press, and a romance all tangled together.
7303-equality:
Edward Bellamy's Equality takes up where Looking Backward left off, using the year 2000 and the earlier story's framework as a starting point. Bellamy explains in his preface that the first book was small. What he left out has since loomed larger than what it contained, so he felt constrained to write another book to say the rest.

The new volume fills in the social order only sketched before, asking how a just commonwealth might run in detail. Bellamy's utopian voice stays earnest and systematic, favouring clear exposition over plot twists. Readers who liked Looking Backward get its fuller, more deliberate sequel here.
7333-sidelights-on-relativity:
Albert Einstein's Sidelights on Relativity joins two addresses. Ether and the Theory of Relativity was given at Leyden on May 5, 1920. Geometry and Experience was expanded from an address to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin on January 27, 1921. The first asks how physicists came to set beside ponderable matter, drawn from everyday life, the idea of another kind of matter, the ether. It seeks the answer in phenomena that gave rise to action at a distance.

Einstein traces how relativity reshaped that old idea rather than simply discarding it, then turns to geometry's relation to physical experience. The two talks together give a short, lucid entry to relativity from its author's own mouth. Readers meet great physics in lecture form, clear and unadorned.
7348-the-jewel-city:
Ben Macomber's Jewel City describes the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in its planning and achievement. Its architecture, sculpture, symbolism, and music, its gardens, palaces, and exhibits appear with a coloured frontispiece and more than seventy-five other illustrations. His introduction quotes a charming Eastern woman of culture walking the Fine Arts colonnade at evening, while searchlights lit Maybeck's masterpiece and the half-domes and arches across the lagoon.

Why, she exclaimed, all the beauty of the world has been sifted, and the finest of it assembled here. Macomber takes that praise as his measure, guiding readers through a fair built to dazzle. The book preserves San Francisco's exposition as a work of art in itself.
7786-the-one-great-reality:
Louisa Clayton's The One Great Reality gathers addresses on the central truths of faith, dedicated to friends at Rusthall after thirty years of gospel fellowship. Evan H. Hopkins adds a foreword praising the clear, attractive way the great topics are set forth, and hoping readers store the messages in their hearts.

Chapters run from God the Great Reality and God our Father through the Son, the Spirit, the voice, the hands, and the Word of God, ending with faith in God. Written from Tunbridge Wells, the book aims at plain, warm teaching for believers seeking a steady ground for daily life.
783-the-lost-city:
Joseph E. Badger Jr. wrote this adventure of Professor Featherwit, a man of science whose notes and experiments lead him to an unknown land. A tornado lifts his party into strange country, where a duel, a queer fish, and unwelcome visitors test their wits. The lost city of the title waits beyond the wilds.

Badger writes in the dime-novel style, with brisk chapters, bold perils, and a hero who thinks his way out of trouble. The tale mixes science fancy with frontier adventure, in the spirit of Verne. It charms readers who enjoy old-fashioned lost-world yarns, where each chapter ends with a fresh wonder or danger.
7886-steam-steel-and-electricity:
James W. Steele's Steam, Steel, and Electricity teaches three forces that remade the modern world, in plain chapters with diagrams. The story of steam runs from Hero's engine and temple doors through Branca, Savery, Papin, Newcomen, and Watt's improvements, crank, governor, and expansive use.

The age of steel follows bronze, lost arts, and oriental steel to cast steel, American iron works, water power, and trip hammers, showing how iron helped win independence. A third part, on electricity, completes a clear primer for young readers on engines, metals, and power, with the workshop made vivid.
8104-the-national-being-some-thoughts-on:
AE, the pen name of George William Russell, addressed these thoughts on an Irish polity to Sir Horace Plunkett, who had grafted a slip of poetry onto his economic tree. Russell warns that the essay may be neither economics in Plunkett's sense nor poetry in his own, but a speculation on how heaven and earth might be brought within hailing distance. His philosophy holds that all are responsible for the results of their actions and their effects on others.

The book argues for a co-operative, spiritually grounded Ireland, where farming, industry, and culture grow together. Written during the Home Rule debates, it shaped Irish thinking about self-government. For readers of Irish history, it remains a visionary and practical text, by a poet who also organised farmers.
8434-the-ladies-a-shining-constellation-:
E. Barrington, in The Ladies, aims not at historical exactitude nor unbending accuracy in dates, but at re-creating the personalities of a succession of charming women. Portraits illustrate the volume, opening with Elizabeth, Duchess of Hamilton and Argyle, née Gunning, one of the famous Gunning sisters whose beauty dazzled London.

Barrington's stories form a gallery of wit and beauty, Georgian and Regency ladies seen through anecdote and imagination. Readers get society history as portraiture, lively and romantic rather than scholarly. The book suits anyone who likes historical biography with color, and who will forgive a storyteller's license for a vivid personality.
862-philosophy-4-a-story-of-harvard-univ:
Owen Wister wrote this story of Harvard, centred on the course called Philosophy 4 and the young men who take it. Two frowning boys in tennis flannels sit beneath lamp and gas, listening with gloomy hunger to a third who tutors them. The scene sets a tale of college work, friendship, and honour.

Wister, himself a Harvard man, writes with humour and affection for undergraduate life, its clubs, its codes, and its trials. The story turns on what young men owe each other and their college, when study and sport collide. It offers a vivid, old-fashioned portrait of Harvard at the turn of the century.
889-two-years-in-the-forbidden-city:
Princess Der Ling, first lady in waiting to the Empress Dowager of China, wrote this memoir of two years inside the Forbidden City. Daughter of Lord Yu Keng of the Manchu White Banner, she entered court life with a rare insider's view, and she dedicates the book to her beloved father.

Der Ling describes the Empress Dowager, court rites, dress, food, and daily routine, with anecdotes that humanise a secluded world. Her account, written for Western readers, blends admiration with candour. The book remains a vivid, first-hand portrait of late Qing court life, just before its fall.
9081-the-bacillus-of-beauty:
Harriet Stark wrote this romance of today around a strange science: a bacillus, or germ, that grants beauty. Its heroine passes from a broken chrysalis to a butterfly, as the chapter titles put it. She becomes the most beautiful woman in the world, and faces mobs, reporters, and lovers in turn.

A girl bachelor and biologist finds the germ, and a great change follows. Love, fame, and loss test the gift to its limits. Stark's tale mixes satire with sentiment, poking fun at a world that worships looks. It is a curious, lively relic of early science romance.
917-barnaby-rudge-a-tale-of-the-riots-of:
Charles Dickens wrote this historical novel about the Gordon Riots of 1780, when London mobs rose against Catholic relief and burned the city for days. Barnaby Rudge, a simple young man with a pet raven named Grip, is drawn into the riots, while his father hides a darker past.

Dickens mixes a murder mystery with the history of the mob, showing how fear and rumour turn crowds to fire. The novel's London, from quiet homes to burning prisons, is vividly drawn. Barnaby Rudge stands as Dickens's first historical novel, and a powerful study of riot, madness, and loyalty.
9172-a-study-of-association-in-insanity:
Grace Helen Kent and A. J. Rosanoff wrote this study at Kings Park State Hospital in New York. It tests how minds link one word to another, first in healthy subjects, then in patients judged insane. Part One sets a normal standard with frequency tables of common replies. Part Two sorts patients' replies by type.

Reactions range from sound links and word completions to neologisms, or made-up words, and full dissociation, where sense breaks down. The work aimed to give doctors a tool for diagnosis. It remains a landmark in early psychology, sober, careful, and humane in method.
9222-a-select-party:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote this fancy piece about a man of fancy who gives a party in a castle in the air. He invites a select number of great personages to his airy mansion, built from a ledge of heavy, sombre clouds. The effect at first looks gloomy, like a feudal fortress or a state prison, not a home of pleasure.

So the owner, regardless of cost, gilds the outside from top to bottom. Hawthorne's jest turns on imagination itself: who gets invited to the mind's feast, and why? The piece remains a witty, light allegory of taste and fame.
9986-wild-kitty:
L. T. Meade's school story introduces Bessie, Alice, Gwin, and Elma, and above all Kitty, the wild girl of the title. Chapters follow the Blarney Stone, tiffs all round, an incorrigible Kitty, and a tug-of-war, in the lively manner of girls' school fiction.

Later adventures bring the little house in Constantine Road, the head mistress and the cabbage-rose, Paddy Wheel-About, the spotted leopard, and a lost packet. Meade writes with humor and warmth for young readers. Girls get a heroine whose high spirits cause trouble, and whose heart wins friends in the end.
a-beautiful-possibility: Edith Ferguson Black opens this novel in a villa on a West Indian island, amid tropical gardens, birds, and fountains. The owner of the house sits writing in his library while the island world moves around him. The novel then follows the household and its visitors through the pleasures and strains of island life. Black builds the tale through vivid scenes of place, social life, and quiet inner conflict.
a-beleaguered-city:
Margaret Oliphant, a Scots writer of great range, wrote this strange tale of a French town in 1880. The town is Semur, a quiet place of old homes and slow days. Oliphant was famed for sober tales of real life, which makes this book stand out.

The dead of the town rise and come back, in a calm and grave host. They drive the living from their homes, yet do no harm and speak no word that men can grasp. The tale's power lies in its hush: a siege by ghosts, told with rare weight and calm.
a-district-messenger-boy-and-a-necktie-p:
A District Messenger Boy and A Necktie Party, by James Otis, collects short tales for boys from the author of Toby Tyler. The first opens in a messenger office, where Joe Curtis, number two hundred ninety seven, receives exact orders from a traveler. He must take tickets to the Sound steamer, claim the key of a paid stateroom, and stow two satchels before the boat sails for Providence within the hour.

From that errand grows the tale of the unwilling passengers, and a second story, Dan Hardy's Crippy, fills out the first half. A Necktie Party then runs three chapters of rival schemes by Si, Aggie, and Tom, each plotting around the same social prize. Otis, who wrote working boys' lives by the shelf, keeps the machinery light: errands, steamers, and party tricks, with every boy's competence quietly on trial.
a-select-party: Nathaniel Hawthorne imagines a man of fancy giving an entertainment in a castle in the air, inviting a select number of distinguished personages. The mansion's foundations and massive walls are quarried from a ledge of heavy, sombre clouds brooding over the earth through an autumnal day. Finding the effect gloomy, like a feudal fortress or monastery, the owner gilds the exterior from top to bottom with gathered evening sunshine.
a-study-of-association-in-insanity: Grace Helen Kent, with A. J. Rosanoff of Kings Park State Hospital, studies association in insanity through word-association tests. The first part sets a normal standard from normal subjects, with method, frequency tables, and associational tendencies. The second part classifies reactions in insane subjects: partial dissociation, sound reactions, word complements, perseveration, neologisms, circumstantial reactions, distraction, and incoherent reactions, with errors of arbitrary standards weighed. The work gives doctors a yardstick for judging test replies in health and in sickness.
a-woman-of-thirty:
Honoré de Balzac begins on a bright Sunday morning in April 1813, in Ellen Marriage's translation, as a worried father hands his beautiful young daughter down from a carriage in Paris. The first part, called Early Mistakes, follows her into a marriage chosen for rank rather than love. Her life becomes the book's long study.

In linked episodes Balzac follows the woman through young love, boredom, a lover, children, loss, and age, watching how each stage changes her heart. Few novels of the period treat a woman's inner life so fully or so unsparingly. The title fixed a phrase in French culture: the woman of thirty, at the height of her powers and sorrows.
america-s-war-for-humanity: Thomas Herbert Russell narrates America's war for humanity, covering the First World War from the battle of Mons onward with pictures of batteries in action. The volume presents the conflict as a struggle for freedom, tracing American forces and their allies. Its popular, patriotic tone suited readers following the war from home.
an-exhortation-to-peace-and-unity:
John Bunyan's treatise takes its text from Ephesians: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. An editorial note in this 1845 printing admits the work's genuineness has been questioned, yet prints it with the collected works, as most editions do. The voice that speaks is Bunyan's in manner, plain and urgent.

Religion, the treatise argues, is the great bond of human society, and it shames Christians when religion itself is split by strife. The writer pleads with believers who hold one Lord, one faith, and one baptism to stop wounding each other over lesser things. The tract is short, warm, and practical, aimed at church quarrels of Bunyan's own hard century.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-in-society:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this volume in 1910. Mrs. Merrick opens fire on Uncle John: he is not doing his duty by those girls. John Merrick, rich and reflective, accepts the charge, and the three nieces prepare for their plunge into fashionable society, with Diana Von Taer as their glittering guide.

Trouble begins with a hero's entrance and deepens around the Von Taer pearls. When the pearls surface in an empty flower vase, impartial judges acquit the accused niece: a Merrick heiress could buy anything and would hardly steal heirlooms anyone might recognise. Madame Cerise, a telephone call, Fogerty the detective, and Diana's revolt carry the mystery. Baum satirises debutante politics while the theft plot tightens toward its crisis.
aunt-mary-s-primer-adorned-with-a-hundre:
An anonymous English primer of 1851, this little book teaches reading with a hundred and twenty pretty pictures, as its title boasts. Frontispiece scenes show angling, shooting, a donkey race, and children at play. A note to the teacher sets the method: once Little Mary knows her letters, pronounce each monosyllable whole — say am at once, never a, m, am.

Lessons climb from letters and one-syllable words to simple readings about the world. The months pass in review: July for haymaking, August for harvest, September for ripe apples, November for London fog, December for Christmas. Large things that we see names houses, churches, barns, water-mills, and wind-mills in captioned pictures. The primer shows early Victorian whole-word teaching in homely, rural dress.
australian-search-party:
Charles H. Eden's Australian Search Party, reprinted from H. W. Bates's Illustrated Travels, begins with a cyclone. In the autumn of 1866 a storm nearly destroyed Cardwell and Townsville on Queensland's north-east coast. Among its losses was the schooner Eva, bound for Rockingham Bay with passengers and cargo. Then came a report of white men seen among the tribes near the Herbert River. Only those who have visited Australia, Eden writes, can picture such captivity's horror. A search party went out to learn the truth.

Eden narrates the expedition into the ranges and scrubs. His pages mix geography, danger, and the period's hard assumptions about the frontier. Readers get a primary document of Australian exploration literature: a rescue that became a survey of unknown country, written by a participant for Bates's great popular record of discovery and adventure.
b09-luther-address-nobility:
Martin Luther aimed his 1520 address, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, straight at the princes of Germany. He argued that Rome had built three walls to guard its power from reform. Behind them, Rome claimed that church rule outranks earthly rule. It claimed that only Rome can read Scripture, and only the pope can call a council.

Luther knocks down each wall in turn and calls on the nobility to act. The address gave the Reformation a clear public program, in German, for lay rulers to carry out. It also stands as a founding text of German national feeling. Few pamphlets of the age reached so far.
b09-luther-babylonian-captivity:
On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, published by Martin Luther in 1520, takes its title from the exile of Israel in Babylon. Luther casts the church of Rome as the captor and the sacraments as the captives. The Latin treatise was the boldest of the three great tracts he issued that year.

Luther cuts the seven sacraments of the old church down to two that he finds clearly set by Christ, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Penance holds a partial place in his scheme. The attack struck at the core of priestly power over daily life. It forms the doctrinal heart of the break with Rome.
barnaby-rudge-a-tale-of-the-riots-of-eig:
Charles Dickens wrote Barnaby Rudge as a tale of the riots of eighty, the Gordon Riots of 1780, and prefaced it with an essay on ravens drawn from two birds he owned. The simple-minded Barnaby, his mother, and his talking raven Grip stand near a fifteen-year-old murder mystery at the Warren. Locksmith Gabriel Varden and his apprentice Joe carry the respectable side of the story.

Secret marriages, a runaway son defended against his mother's scorn, and Protestant mobs marching on London build toward the riots' fire and slaughter. Dickens, writing early in his career, made this his first historical novel. Its crowd scenes and study of fanaticism still impress, and Grip later echoed into Poe's famous raven.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-04-imper:
John Lord's fourth Beacon Lights volume treats imperial antiquity through two conquerors. Cyrus the Great opens it, under the heading Asiatic Supremacy. Contents cover Persia's religion, Cyrus's youth and schooling, and the union of Persia and Media. Then come Croesus of Lydia, the taking of Babylon, and his kindness to the Jews. Julius Caesar follows as the type of imperialism, judged an instrument of Providence.

Later lectures reach Roman society and its women. One passage sets woman's mission as administering the antidote to evil: labour made sweet, pain assuaged, courage fortified, and duty sacred. Paula is praised for proving a pure and lofty friendship possible beyond the pollutions and slaveries of the ancient world. Lord moralises empire freely, reading conquest as a stage in a providential plan that ends in Christian Rome.
beasley-s-christmas-party:
Beasley's Christmas Party, by Booth Tarkington, follows a young newspaperman through his first days in a state capital. Tarkington dates the tale October 1909 and dedicates it to the poet James Whitcomb Riley. The narrator returns at four in the morning from his first night's work on the Wainwright Morning Despatch. Moonlit streets lie still as a country Sunday. He passes the house he most admires in the city.

He has just taken a room next door at Mrs Apperthwaite's, and counts the fine house almost a citizen's possession. From that doorstep he is drawn into the world of Beasley, a local magnate. Beasley's Christmas party mixes politics, money, and a household secret. The secret involves an imaginary companion. Tarkington tells it as comedy with a sting: a small capital's great man, a reporter's education, and the season when every performance of generosity is also a move in the game.
beyond-the-city:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote Beyond the City in 1892, a short novel of the new suburbs south of London, written between his Sherlock Holmes tales. It opens with two elderly sisters, Monica and Bertha, watching from behind their curtain as new neighbors move into the villa across the road. The newcomers, a widow's household lately rich from India, stir the quiet street of three neat houses.

Courtships form among the young people, money worries surface, and a secret from the Indian past works its way into the present. Doyle, who lived in such a suburb himself at Norwood, draws the tea tables, lawns, and gossip with affection and a light sting. The tale shows his gift working without a detective to lead it.
black-beauty:
Anna Sewell wrote Black Beauty, published in 1877, her only book, written in ill health during the last years of her life. The story is told by the horse himself. Beauty begins as a glossy black colt on a kind farm. He learns his lessons from his mother. Then he is sold from home to home. Some owners are kind, and some are careless. He works as a carriage horse, a cab horse in London, and a cart horse worn nearly to death.

His stable mates, merry Merrylegs and high-spirited Ginger, meet fates of their own. Sewell wrote the book to protest cruelty to horses. She hated the tight bearing rein then in fashion. The book changed how a nation treated its animals, and it still speaks for them.
bohemian-society:
Lydia Leavitt wrote Bohemian Society, printed at Brockville by the Times Printing and Publishing Company. Leavitt frames the work as talks at a country house near a city, where a learned hostess gathers guests with ideas. Artists, authors, spiritualists, and thinkers speak in turn.

One guest dreams aloud of a valley Utopia where no one is richer than a neighbor and money counts for nothing. A cynic answers with a hard look at shoddy wealth and dress judged by cost. Other voices weigh faith, science, and reform in the manner of Tyndall, Huxley, and Spencer. The talk form lets each view clash in the open. Readers get a Canadian parlor debate on how people ought to live together.
britannica-1911-aberdeen-city:
Aberdeen as a city receives a second entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. Harbour works lead: Smeaton's and Telford's north pier runs near 3,000 feet into the North Sea, and the Victoria Dock of 1848 gives 6,000 feet of quay. The Dee was diverted for the Albert Basin in 1868.

Granite quarried three hundred years now yields to deep-sea fishing, boosted by beam trawling from 1882, as the growth trade. Woollens, linen, cotton, and paper, first made here in 1694, fill old mills. Clippers of tea-race fame recall the wooden-ship days. Charters from David the First and William the Lion open a history of burning, plunder by both sides in the civil wars, and Jacobite visits. Growth from 3,000 souls in 1396 to 153,503 in 1901 closes the account.
britannica-1911-agriculture-food-values-:
Food-values and Early Maturity, a section of the Agriculture article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, draws on feeding trials carried out at Rothamsted. Its question is what part of an animal's feed actually builds new live weight. The answer given stresses digestible non-nitrogenous matter, the feed parts other than nitrogen compounds, over the nitrogenous parts.

Fat laid down by a growing animal, the section argues, comes mainly from non-nitrogenous feed. Only a small share of feed nitrogen stays in the body, while most passes through and remains for manure. Later pages turn to early maturity in meat animals and to show classes for cattle, sheep, and pigs, listing beef breeds from Devon and Hereford to Aberdeen-Angus and Highland.
britannica-1911-badajoz-city:
Badajoz is the capital of its Spanish province, set close to the Portuguese frontier on the left bank of the river Guadiana along the Madrid to Lisbon railway. Its 30,899 people in 1900 live under a ruined Moorish castle on a small rise, ringed by walls, bastions, and a broad moat.

Even the cathedral of 1258 looks like a fortress with its massive battlements. The town was painter Morales's and statesman Godoy's birthplace. Unmentioned by Roman writers, Badajoz rose under Moorish rule and headed a small Moorish kingdom from 1031 until Leon took it in 1229. Frontier sieges fill its later story, ending with Wellington's storming of the fortress in April 1812 at terrible loss.
britannica-1911-bagdad-city:
Bagdad, or Baghdad, is the capital of the Turkish vilayet of the same name. It is headquarters of the Sixth Army Corps. The city stands on both banks of the river Tigris, in a wide desert plain. Here the Tigris and Euphrates draw nearest, little more than twenty-five miles apart, joined by canal.

The old city on the west bank is now a suburb of 146 walled acres; the greater city on the east shore covers 591 acres. Brick walls with great round towers and a deep ditch once ringed both parts. They fell into decay and were quarried for bricks. Midhat Pasha, governor from 1868 to 1872, finally pulled them down. Periodic floods, fed by the canal system, can turn Bagdad into an island and threaten its dikes.
britannica-1911-bahia-city:
Bahia, or São Salvador, is a maritime city of Brazil. It is capital of the state of Bahia. The city stands on the Bay of All Saints. A peninsula there parts the bay from the Atlantic. Its people numbered about 200,000 in 1900. Two towns stack here: a narrow commercial strip along the water, and an upper town on the bluffs.

The lower town holds arsenal, exchange, custom-house, and market on badly paved streets. Elevators, a circular tramway, and steep zigzag roads climb to the upper town's wider streets, churches, schools, law and medical academies, governor's palace, and a public garden overlooking the bay. The harbour ranks among South America's best and most reachable, drawing coastwise and foreign trade. Thomé de Souza founded the city in 1549 as Brazil's first Portuguese capital seat.
britannica-1911-baker-city:
Baker City is a city in eastern Oregon, America. It seats Baker county there. Portland lies about 337 miles west. The town counted 6,663 people in 1900. By 1910 it held 6,742. Two railways serve the place.

The town stands in the Powder river valley. Blue Mountains rise at its base. Its height is about 3,440 feet. It is eastern Oregon's largest city. Mining interests centre on it. Lumber, farming, and livestock matter too. Settlers laid it out in 1865. It became county-seat in 1868. A city charter followed in 1874. County and city honour Edward Dickinson Baker. He was an orator, soldier, and senator. A London birth began his American life. Ball's Bluff killed him in 1861.
britannica-1911-barrier-treaty:
Barrier Treaty is the name given in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica to agreements meant to shield the Dutch Netherlands from France. The first was signed on 29 October 1709 between Great Britain and the Dutch states-general. The Dutch would back the Protestant succession in England for the house of Hanover. In return, Britain would win them a line of strong frontier towns against French attack.

Later treaties cut that line down. A second treaty in January 1713 listed fewer strong places, among them Ypres, Menin, Tournai, Mons, and Charleroi, and its terms passed into the Treaty of Rastatt in 1714. A third Barrier Treaty followed in November 1715. Behind all three stood the older idea, already used at Ryswick in 1698, that Dutch troops garrisoning frontier fortresses could keep Holland safe.
britannica-1911-basel-city:
Basel, called Bâle in French and Basilea in Italian, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the capital of the Swiss half canton of Basel Stadt. It was then the second most populous town in Switzerland after Zürich, with 109,161 inhabitants, and reputed the richest. The entry credits the St Gotthard railway, opened in 1882, for much of that wealth, since goods from across northern and central Europe were stored in Basel before redistribution south.

River and buildings shape the city portrait. The Rhine divides Gross Basel to the south from Klein Basel to the north, joined by several bridges. The red sandstone cathedral, consecrated in 1019 and largely rebuilt after the earthquake of 1356, held the public meetings of the Council of Basel. Erasmus lived here and is buried in the cathedral. The museum holds fine works by Holbein, and the university, founded in 1460, is called the oldest in Switzerland.
britannica-1911-batavia-city:
Batavia, a city and seaport on the north coast of Java, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the capital of all the Dutch settlements in the East. It held 115,567 people in 1898, among them Europeans, Chinese, and Arabs. The town stands on both banks of the Jacatra river in a swampy plain at the head of a wide bay. Broad, tree-lined streets and canals cut through much of it.

Old and new towns stand in contrast. The old town, once walled, had lost its ramparts, and its great European houses had decayed into stores; only Malays, Arabs, and Chinese still lived there. Europeans moved to the new town on higher, healthier ground, built up from suburbs such as Weltevreden and Rijswijk. There stood the governor-general's palace, the barracks, and the hospitals of the colonial government.
britannica-1911-bay-city:
Bay City is a city of Michigan, in the United States, and the seat of Bay county, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Saginaw river, about two miles from Saginaw Bay and 108 miles north-north-west of Detroit. Its people numbered 27,628 in 1900 and leapt to 45,166 in 1910, many of them foreign-born: English-Canadians, Germans, Poles, who had their own weekly paper, and French-Canadians. Four railways and lake steamers serve the city, which runs for miles along both banks of the river.

Wood, fish, and salt built the town. Bay City holds lumber and fishing interests, the bay yielding perch, whitefish, sturgeon, and other fish. Its machine shops and foundries made nearly a third of its factory output in 1905. A salt bed lies under the city. Salt was the first trade raised after lumber, but its share later shrank.
britannica-1911-bern-city:
Bern, capital of its canton and, by federal law of 1848, political capital of the Swiss Confederation, stands on a high peninsula looped by the river Aar. The 1911 Britannica article picks out its arcaded main street, its ornate fountains, and two old towers, including the Zeitglockenthurm with its famous 16th-century mechanical clock.

The chief church is the Münster, begun in 1421 and finished in 1573, though Bern never had a bishop and it was never a cathedral. The federal parliament buildings, enlarged in 1888–1892, hold the federal executive offices. The article ends with the city's history and a long list of Bernese chronicles and histories.
britannica-1911-bokhara-city:
Bokhara, called Bokhara-i-Sherif, is the capital of the state of Bokhara in central Asia. It stands on the left bank of the Zarafshan and on the Shahri-rud irrigation canal, in a rich plain 162 miles by rail west of Samarkand. A stone wall 28 feet high and 8 miles long, with eleven gates, rings the city.

The present city was begun in 830, destroyed by Jenghiz Khan in 1220, and rebuilt after. It holds no fewer than 360 mosques and 140 theological colleges teaching some 10,000 pupils, though its water supply is called very unhealthy. The Mir-Arab mosque and the great brick minaret, 203 feet high, are singled out. Trade in silk, copper ware, lamb skins, and carpets made it central Asia's chief trading town.
britannica-1911-bombay-city:
Bombay City, capital of Bombay Presidency and chief seaport of western India, stands on an island joined by causeways to the mainland. The island covers 22 square miles. Its people numbered 776,006 in 1901 and an estimated 977,822 in 1906, making it the second city of the Indian empire behind Calcutta.

Its site, nearest India to Europe, its harbour, railways, and grip on the cotton trade are set against the poorer farmland behind it, with no great river like the Ganges. The approach by sea is praised as one of the world's finest views. The long entry then covers the harbour islands, climate, streets, trade, cotton mills, government, and the city's growth under Portuguese and then British rule.
britannica-1911-broach-city:
Broach, or Bharuch, is an ancient city and modern district of British India in the northern division of Bombay. The city stands on the right bank of the Nerbudda, about 30 miles from the sea and 203 miles north of Bombay. With its suburbs it covers about 22 square miles and held 42,896 people in 1901. Sea trade is small, a few coasting vessels only.

Handloom weaving is almost dead, but cotton mills and large flour mills have opened in its place. Names track its age: Broach is the Barakacheva of the Chinese traveller Hsuan Tsang and the Barygaza of Ptolemy and Arrian. Muslim conquest folded it into Gujarat, Akbar annexed it to the Mogul empire in 1572, Mahrattas took it in 1685, British forces stormed it in 1772 and again in 1803. It was finally ceded to the East India Company by Sindhia.
britannica-1911-brunswick-german-city:
Brunswick is a German city, capital of the duchy of that name, set in fertile, rolling country on the river Oker, 37 miles south-east of Hanover and 53 north-west of Magdeburg. On the main Berlin railway line. Its people rose from 128,226 in 1900 to 136,423 in 1905, about 9000 of them Roman Catholics and 1000 Jews. Much medieval character survives in the place.

Fortifications dismantled in 1797 gave way to a regular circle of gardens and promenades counted among the finest in Germany. Inside lies the old town of narrow, crooked streets and many ancient houses with high gables and quaintly carved fronts, rivalling Lubeck and Luneburg for picturesqueness among North German towns. Its cathedral, St Blasius, a Romanesque structure begun by Henry the Lion about 1173 and finished in 1194, holds 12th-century frescoes, the tombs of its founder and his consort. That of the emperor Otto IV, with Guelph remains in the vault below.
britannica-1911-capua-ancient-city:
Capua was the chief ancient city of Campania, in Italy. Its modern site is Santa Maria di Capua Vetere. This long 1911 Britannica article gives its full history. It stood 16 miles north of Neapolis. It lay on the north-east edge of the Campanian plain. Its ground was not naturally defensible. Its plan was strikingly regular for an old town. Cato credited its founding to the Etruscans.

The founding date works out at about 600 B.C. That was the height of Etruscan power in Campania. The name probably comes from campus, a plain. Other derivations from a vulture or from caput are rejected. The article follows the city under Etruscans and Samnites. It treats its submission to Rome in 338 B.C. Its part in the Punic Wars gets full treatment. Hannibal's winter stay there is a famous episode. The later empire and the Saracen destruction close the story.
britannica-1911-carlow-county:
Carlow is a county of Ireland, in the province of Leinster. Excepting Louth, it is the smallest county in Ireland. Its area is about 346 square miles. This 1911 Britannica article surveys the county. Kildare and Wicklow bound it on the north. Wexford lies east and south of it. Queen's County and Kilkenny lie to the west. The surface is level or gently undulating in general.

A ridge at Old Leighlin breaks that gentle pattern. Granite heights rise in the south-east of the county. Mount Leinster reaches 2610 feet there. Glacial deposits spread over the lower grounds of Carlow. Eskers, or gravel ridges, show near Bagenalstown in fine form. The county has no lakes and no canals. The river Barrow crosses its western side from north to south. It is navigable through the county to Waterford port. The Slaney forms part of the eastern border.
britannica-1911-carson-city:
Carson City is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the capital of Nevada and the county seat of Ormsby county, about 120 miles north-east of Sacramento, California. Its population was 2466 in 1910, down from 3950 in 1890. The Virginia and Truckee railway serves the city and keeps repair shops there, and a stage runs to Lake Tahoe, 12 miles west. The city sits in Eagle valley near the east base of the Sierra Nevada, 4720 feet above the sea.

Public buildings include the capitol, a United States government building, a mint, and a state orphans' home, with the state prison nearby. The city distributes goods to the surrounding mining region, and its industries rest on mining, lumbering, and farming. It was settled in 1851 as a trading post, laid out in 1858, and made capital and county seat in 1861. It took its name in honour of Christopher Carson and was chartered as a city in 1875.
britannica-1911-cavan-county:
Cavan is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a county in the province of Ulster, Ireland. Fermanagh and Monaghan bound it in the north, Meath in the east and south, and Longford and Leitrim in the west. Its area is 477,399 acres, about 746 square miles. The surface is uneven hill and dale with little level ground. Only in the north does it turn mountainous, where Cuilcagh reaches 2188 feet.

The county holds many lakes, generally small but often beautiful. Lough Oughter, formed by the river Erne, is noted for its inlets and islands. The Erne is the chief river, rising near Lough Gowna and flowing north past Killashandra and Belturbet. The Shannon Pot, a strong spring at the foot of Cuilcagh, is regarded as the source of the Shannon. The Blackwater also rises in the county. The entry adds the woods, the good fishing, and the mineral springs of the district.
britannica-1911-chihuahua-city:
Chihuahua is a city of Mexico and capital of the state of that name, set on the Chihuahua river about 1,000 miles north-west of Mexico City. Its people rose from 18,279 in 1895 to 30,405 in 1900, and it stands 4,635 feet above sea level in a valley hemmed by spurs of the Sierra Madre. Broad streets and a handsome plaza mark its regular plan. A monument there honours Hidalgo and his companions, executed here after the 1810 rising.

The parish church of San Francisco, begun in 1717 and finished in 1789, is praised as fine 18th century work, paid for by a tax on the Santa Eulalia mine. Mining rules the district, that famous mine lying about 12 miles away, and fruit growing comes next. Cotton weaving, a mint, an aqueduct and a railway station fill out the account. Founded as a mining town between 1703 and 1705, the city later served Juárez as a provisional capital in 1864.
britannica-1911-city:
City, through French cité from Latin civitas, is in the United Kingdom strictly an honorary title for certain towns. Royal charter or traditional usage gives that right, for pre-eminence as episcopal sees or great industrial centres. The style does not necessarily bring greater municipal power than an ordinary borough has, nor even a corporation at all, as Ely shows. In the United States and British colonies, by contrast, city rank depends on municipal privileges held.

Common usage is looser, implying only a vague idea of size and dignity for any large centre of population. London is properly called the largest city in the world, though the technical City of London is quite small. France and England both use the word for the old central nucleus of a large town, as the Cité in Paris. The word resists any clear, inclusive definition apart from town or borough.
britannica-1911-ciudad-real-city:
Ciudad Real is the capital of its province in central Spain, 107 miles south of Madrid, on railways to Badajoz, Lisbon and Manzanares. Its people numbered 15,255 in 1900, and it lies amid a wide plain watered north by the Guadiana and south by its tributary the Jabalón. Remnants of 13th century fortifications and one huge Gothic church built without aisles are its chief sights. Other public buildings are called in no way distinguished above those of other provincial capitals.

No important manufactures belong to the town, and trade rests chiefly on weekly sales of farm produce and live stock. Alphonso X of Castile founded it and fortified it as a check on Moorish power, the entry says. Its first name, Villarreal, became Ciudad Real under John in 1420, though the text prints that king as John VI. A Spanish force was defeated here by the French on 27 March 1809, during the Peninsular War.
britannica-1911-clare-county:
Clare is a county in Munster, Ireland, bounded by Galway Bay, Lough Derg, the Shannon, its estuary and the Atlantic Ocean. Its area is 852,389 acres, or nearly 1,332 square miles of mostly hilly country. The west holds much bog land in Moyarta and Ibrickan, while the east mixes mountains with tracts of rich pasture. Along the Fergus and Shannon lie rich low grounds called corcasses, deep loam bands of varied breadth.

Black corcasses suit tillage and blue corcasses suit meadow better, the entry distinguishes in its soil account. The coast is generally rocky and at the cliffs of Moher rises sheer to 580 feet at O'Brien's Tower. Bays at Ballyvaghan, Liscannor and Malbay indent that coast, yet no safe harbour exists along the whole Atlantic side except Liscannor Bay. Malbay takes its name from its dangers to navigators, and many fatal disasters mark the shore.
britannica-1911-clonakilty:
Clonakilty is a seaport and market town of County Cork, Ireland, at the head of Clonakilty Bay, 33 miles south-west of Cork. Its urban district counted 3,098 people in 1901, and a branch of the Cork, Bandon and South Coast railway serves it. Richard Boyle, first earl of Cork, brought it into prosperity, and a charter came in 1613. Part of the town was demolished in a fight between English and Irish in 1641.

The town returned two members to the Irish parliament until the union, and an extensive linen industry flourished in the 18th century. Present trade centres in brewing, corn milling, yarn and farm produce, the entry says. A bar obstructs the harbour mouth, but a pier for large vessels stands at Ring, a mile below the town. Fisheries matter, and a ruined church, castles and a stone circle are the chief antiquities nearby.
britannica-1911-cochabamba-city:
Cochabamba is a city of Bolivia, capital of its department and of the province of Cercado, on the Rocha river at 17 degrees 27 minutes south. Its people numbered 21,886 in 1900, mostly Indians and mestizos, and it stands 8,400 feet above sea level in a broad valley of the Bolivian plateau. Snow clad heights of Tunari and Larati overshadow it. Rough mountain roads join it to Sucre and Oruro, with a subsidised stage coach line to Oruro.

Climate is mild and temperate and the surrounding country fertile and cultivated, suiting the city well. Cochabamba is often described as the most progressive city of Bolivia, yet its isolated situation has held it back. Warehouses hold foreign goods and trade is active despite high prices, and telegraph links run via Oruro. A large part of the Amazon trade reaches it through small river ports, and it holds a university, many churches and a missionary college.
britannica-1911-cromarty:
Cromarty is a police burgh and seaport in the county of Ross and Cromarty in Scotland. Its population in 1901 was 1,242. It stands on the southern shore of the mouth of Cromarty Firth, with a daily steamer to Invergordon. Before the union of the shires it was the county town of Cromartyshire. Its harbour holds the herring fleet, though the fisheries, once the staple trade, have declined.

The town keeps the thatched house in Church Street where the geologist Hugh Miller was born, with a statue to his memory. Cromarty House stands east of the burgh on the site of the old castle of the earls of Ross. The entry then treats Cromarty as a former county, joined to Ross-shire in 1889. That county was built from scattered estates won by the Mackenzies, and it covered nearly 370 square miles. Sir Thomas Urquhart, translator of Rabelais, was born there too.
britannica-1911-donegal-county:
Donegal is a county in the extreme north-west of Ireland, in Ulster, bounded by the Atlantic, Lough Foyle, and the counties of Londonderry, Tyrone, Fermanagh and Leitrim. At about 1871 square miles it is the largest Irish county after Cork and Mayo. The article stresses its poverty of natural wealth and its hard communications. Its fine scenery stayed almost unknown until late in the nineteenth century, when Lord George Hill tried to draw outside wealth in.

The coast is cut by many inlets: Killybegs harbour takes large vessels, Sheephaven and Mulroy Bay shelter the largest ships, and Lough Swilly runs far inland. Islands stud the shore, North Aran the largest of them. Ruined castles, abbeys and the Raphoe cathedral close the gazetteer's survey.
britannica-1911-down-county:
Down is a maritime county of Ireland in Ulster, the most easterly in the island, bounded by Antrim, Belfast Lough, the Irish Sea and Armagh. Its area is nearly 950 square miles, and Strangford Lough, studded with 260 islets, cuts deep into its coast. Between Strangford and Carlingford loughs rise the Mourne Mountains, whose chief peak, Slieve Donard, climbs 2796 feet straight from the sea. The Bann, Lagan, Annacloy and Newry are its principal rivers.

Silurian slates form the county's foundation, with granite running from Newry to Slieve Croob and the younger Mourne granite to the south. Holy wells and mineral springs abound. The article ends among antiquities: Saul Abbey, Inch Abbey of 1180, Downpatrick's cathedral, and three fragmentary round towers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-administrator:
An administrator of church property is one charged with the care of church goods. Supreme administrative authority over all church temporalities rests with the Sovereign Pontiff, by his primacy of jurisdiction. The pope's power here is solely administrative, since he cannot properly be called owner of goods belonging to the universal church or particular churches.

Pontifical authority works chiefly via the Propaganda, St. Peter's Fabrica, the Camera Apostolica, and the Cardinal Camerlengo, and appears in decrees of councils worldwide. In each diocese, administration rests primarily with the bishop, subject to the Holy See, and all inferior administrators depend on him unless exempted by law, as with religious orders. Parish priests bear an important share of this duty, and councils urge administrators to secure titles under secular law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-cavity:
The altar cavity is a small chamber, square or oblong, in the altar's body holding relics of two canonized martyrs. One martyr's relic alone still makes the consecration valid, and other saints' relics may be added, especially the saint honoured by the church. The relics must be real portions of the saints' bodies, not merely of their garments.

The chamber may sit at the altar's front or back, midway between table and foot, or in the table's centre near the front edge. A bevelled stone slab fits exactly over the opening when the first or second place is chosen. Sealed within, the relics belong to the altar's consecration rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amovibility:
Canon law gives the name amovibility to the state of church officers who can be removed from their posts at a bishop's will. Most rectors in the United States and England fall in this class. Parish assistants, vicars-general, archdeacons, and rural deans belong there too, while holders of perpetual dignities can lose office only in set cases.

Canonists long argued over whether a bishop could remove such a man without cause. Exceptions arose where hatred, damage to a good name, or harm to a parish was involved. The article sets out the limits on that power and the right of recourse to a higher authority. It also gives the procedure laid down for the United States by the Second Plenary Council of Baltimore and later Roman instructions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-maj:
Apostolic Majesty is a title borne by the kings of Hungary. It has been used since Maria Theresa's time by the king himself and in letters addressed to him by officials and private persons. Its supposed origin lies with St. Stephen, said to have gained it from Pope Sylvester II for spreading Christianity in Hungary. Hartvik, Stephen's biographer, reports the pope hailing him as a veritable apostle of Christ for his holy labours in the faith.

Yet Sylvester's bull of 27 March 1000 granted Stephen crown and royal title. It also returned the kingdom he had offered to Rome and gave him the right to have the cross borne before him with authority over bishoprics. Even so, it gives no basis for this particular title. Moreover, that bull is proved a forgery later than 1574. The entry thus separates a proud royal style from the shaky document once used to support it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicity:
Apostolicity is the mark by which today's church is recognized as identical with the church Jesus founded upon the apostles. It matters most, the article argues, because it is the surest sign of the true church, the easiest to examine, and it virtually contains unity, sanctity, and catholicity. Apostolic is preferred to Christian because it links church to Christ its founder and to the apostles.

An apostle is one sent by Christ's authority to continue his mission, above all a member of the Twelve. Apostolicity of doctrine and of mission are both required. Doctrine demands that the deposit of faith entrusted to the apostles be kept whole, and mission demands a line of envoys from them. The entry gives the Catholic logic of a church that claims to be not merely old, but apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
An archconfraternity is a group empowered to affiliate other groups of the same kind and to share with them its indulgences and privileges. The article sets out what a reader needs to grasp the general subject. It covers what must come first, the rules for joining, the usual method of the process, and a list of the main groups.

To gain indulgences, the group to be joined must first be approved and given legal existence by proper church authority. Archconfraternities do not set groups up; they merely join them. That approval normally belongs to the local bishop, though heads of certain religious orders hold the power for many groups, above all in mission lands or abnormal conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aseity:
Aseity, from Latin a, from, and se, itself, meaning being from itself, is the property by which a being subsists of and from itself. It belongs, and can belong only, to God, the article argues. Seeking the efficient, exemplary, and final cause of every thing, of their existence, nature, and organization, we reach at last a Being. He depends for existence, realization, or end on no cause but himself. He holds within himself his own reason for being.

That property of absolute independence, or self-existence in nature, is what we call aseity. The notion holds a negative and a positive side, absolute independence and self-existence, which together form one single objective property. The Catholic concept presents God as independent and self-existent by nature, not merely uncaused by accident, and the entry unpacks a short Latin term into a whole doctrine of God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-bonn:
Augustin Bonnetty was a French writer born at Entrevaux in 1798 who died at Paris in 1879. He entered the Digne seminary in 1815, but, too young for ordination, he tutored a family at Marseilles. He soon felt his mission was to defend the Church with science and philosophy while remaining a layman. In Paris in 1830 he founded the Annales de Philosophie Chretienne, which he edited until his death. Its aim was to show the agreement of science and religion.

A chief theme was a primitive revelation, said to be visible even in the myths of all nations. Bonnetty pressed this idea too far, stressing revelation and slighting reason, a drift toward traditionalism that drew Rome's notice. In 1855 he was asked to sign four propositions guarding reason's role in reaching truth. His books included Beauties of Church History, Christianity and Philosophy, and a translation of Premare's traces of Christian dogma in Chinese books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baker-city:
Baker City is a diocese covering fifteen Oregon counties, an area of 65,683 square miles. It was established in 1903, and Charles J. O'Reilly became its first bishop that year. O'Reilly, rector of Portland's Immaculate Heart of Mary and editor of the Catholic Sentinel, was consecrated on 25 August. The diocese counted about 4,000 Catholics, served by ten diocesan and seven Franciscan and Jesuit priests.

Sisters of St Francis, St Dominic, and the Holy Name ran five schools and academies. At the Umatilla reservation, over 500 Catholic Indians were served by Jesuits, two teaching brothers, and eight Franciscan sisters. The diocese held thirteen churches and thirty-six mission stations. O'Reilly was born at St John, New Brunswick, in 1862, studied at Montreal's Grand Seminary, and was ordained at Portland in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capital-punis:
Capital punishment is death inflicted by lawful process as a penalty for crime. The entry traces the practice from the earliest human history through ancient Israel and Rome to modern states. The Latin word capitalis, tied to caput or head, covered whatever touched life itself. The entry opens with Cain's fratricide and the decree of Genesis 9:6.
