It follows with the many capital offenses in the law given to Israel.

Later sections follow Roman statutes on poisoning and conspiracy and English witchcraft laws that claimed thousands of victims. They note canon law's bar on clerics shedding blood. They weigh reformers such as Beccaria and Voltaire against the penalty. The entry closes with methods around the world, from beheading in Switzerland and Prussia to shooting in Ecuador and Oldenburg. Spain used the garrotte, and China strangled offenders in public.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chastity:
An entry on chastity as a virtue, the control of sexual appetite by reason, treated here apart from celibacy and virginity, which have their own articles. Chastity belongs to temperance, the virtue that governs pleasures, and stands beside abstinence and sobriety, which govern food and drink. It is often confused with modesty, but modesty is properly its outpost and safeguard, a reserve about acts that cause shame.

Aristotle marked a line between chastity and continence. The entry traces the virtue from nature, where reason alone checks appetite, to faith, where the body is honoured as the temple of the Holy Spirit. It surveys Greek and Roman practice, where sexual licence was open and marriage lightly broken. Christian practice then made chastity stern and austere, through the example of Christ and the image of marriage as the union of Christ and the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christianity:
A vast entry on Christianity as a religion, setting out its origin, its relation to other faiths, and its essential nature. It leaves doctrines in detail and the Church as a visible organisation to separate articles. It speaks of the Christianity realised in the Catholic Church alone, not of non-Catholic sects.

Its sources are chiefly the New Testament and writings just after the apostles, whose authenticity the entry takes as largely granted, as historians grant Caesar on Gaul or Tacitus on Rome. It notes that mature non-Catholic critics now place the Gospels, Acts, and most Epistles in the apostolic age. Harnack is quoted on the fullness of tradition already present under Trajan, between 98 and 117.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-proper:
An entry on church property, defending the Church's right to acquire and hold temporal goods. Though acted on everywhere, that right met contradictors: Arnold of Brescia, the Waldenses, Marsilius of Padua, and the Wycliffites held that Gospel ministers should own nothing. John the Twenty-second answered Marsilius in 1323, affirming that Christ and the apostles truly owned what they held and that church goods were not at the emperor's disposal.

Constance condemned Wyclif and Hus, defining that churchmen may hold possessions without sin and that civil seizure counts as sacrilege. Pius the Ninth reaffirmed the point in Quanta Cura of 1864, rejecting any claim that state ownership of all church property squares with theology or canon law. Beyond decrees, the entry grounds the right in reason and tradition: a visible society with public duties needs temporal means, and gifts bestowed on the Church remain under her control.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-authori:
Civil authority, the moral power of command, is backed when needed by physical coercion over its members, exercised by the State. The article treats its nature, sources, limits, divisions, and origin, with true and false theories. Authority is natural to man because man naturally lives in society, and society holds together only under authority. Even professed anarchists, it argues, treat anarchy as a temporary step toward their own rule.

Forms of government vary endlessly: monarchies, aristocracies, and democracies, direct like ancient Athens or representative like the United States. The fixed point is that the authority actually existing must be obeyed, since refusing it means refusing authority itself. The article then weighs contract theories, including Hobbes and his Leviathan and Rousseau and his General Will, against the older teaching on authority's origin and bounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-incorpo:
Christianity found the corporation already developed under Roman law and adapted it early to hold and transmit church property. Second- and third-century burial societies served this end, and great medieval monasteries were organised as corporations. Mortmain law shows how secure this tenure proved amid feudal warfare. Canon lawyers refined the idea into the corporation sole: a bishop, vicar, or pastor who succeeds to an office and its temporal goods alone.

In England corporations arise by prescription, charter, or parliamentary Act; in the United States a state legislature creates them. American law treats church and incorporated religious society as different things, the society handling temporal goods. Title often stays with the bishop in fee simple, but states trend toward incorporation, as in New York in 1863 and Michigan in 1897. English Catholics before the Charity Act of 1832 could only trust private holders, with no legal remedy if they misused a bequest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clandestinity:
Clandestinity is the matrimonial impediment Trent introduced by the decree Tametsi. Anyone attempting marriage otherwise than before the parish priest, or another priest with his or the ordinary's leave, and before two or three witnesses, is rendered incapable of the contract. Such a contract is null and void. The council upheld earlier clandestine marriages until annulled, yet declared the Church always abhorred and prohibited them.

That antipathy runs back to Ignatius of Antioch, who urged marriage with the bishop's consent, and to Tertullian, who judged unions without church authority near fornication. A Fourth Council of Carthage canon, so called, required presentation to a priest for blessing. The decree's reach varied with promulgation. It was never published in England, Scotland, or Scandinavia, and Benedict the Fourteenth settled its application to Dutch heretics. Delegation of the priest's faculty, special or general, raised further questions of validity and liceity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-columbia-univ:
John McGinn's entry describes Columbia University at Portland, Oregon, not the New York school of the same name. It stands on the east bank of the Willamette in northern Portland. The Congregation of Holy Cross runs it, from its mother-house at Notre Dame, Indiana. In 1898 Portland University, run by a local Methodist group, failed and closed. Its buildings stood empty for three years. In 1901 Archbishop Alexander Christie bought the property for the diocese.

For one year diocesan clergy ran the school, now called Columbia University. In 1902 Christie asked the Holy Cross provincial, Rev. J. A. Zahm, for teachers, and religious soon took charge. The university gained incorporation under Oregon law in 1909, with power to grant degrees in arts, sciences, and letters. By 1912 about two hundred students studied there under twenty professors. New Christie Hall added room for one hundred and fifty more.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
William Fanning's entry defines a confraternity or sodality, from Latin confraternitas, as a voluntary association of the faithful. Competent church authority erects and guides it for special works of Christian charity or piety. Pious unions resemble confraternities, but differ in two ways. They need not be canonically erected. They also seek the neighbor's good rather than members' personal sanctification. Confraternities split into those properly so called and those bearing the name by extension.

Both kinds rise by canonical authority. Proper confraternities hold a more precise organization, with rights and duties set by church law. Members often wear a peculiar costume and recite the Office together. When a confraternity gains power to aggregate other sodalities, its reach widens further. Lay associations of this sort stood at Constantinople and Alexandria in very ancient times. Clement VIII's constitution of 7 December 1604, later modified, still frames much of their law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Brother Philemon's entry follows the Brothers of Charity, founded in Belgium early in the present century. Leo XIII approved and confirmed rule and constitutions on 4 July 1899. Founder Pierre J. Triest, titular canon of Saint Bavon of Ghent, earned the name Vincent de Paul of his country for charity's service, winning three royal decorations with the land's highest civic orders. After his death countrymen raised a superb Brussels mausoleum in his honor.

The congregation aims first at members' sanctification in religious life through charity embracing every phase of moral and physical suffering and want. Works center on tending the sick, sheltering poor workmen, and caring for the aged and the insane. Government rests with a superior general at Ghent, cradle of the congregation, aided by a four-member central council, assistant visitors, a general secretary, and a general procurator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consanguinity:
Richard Burtsell's entry defines consanguinity as a marriage impediment reaching the fourth degree inclusive. The term means blood-relationship, the bond between persons descended from the same stock, within limits set by nature, God, or State or Church. Since all men descend from one stock, limitation points to the nearest root.

Descent of one from another forms the direct line; shared blood from a common ancestor, the collateral. History traces groups marrying within themselves, early Rome forbidding cousin marriage, though frequent after the Second Punic War, with discipline continuing to the eighth century. A Germanic computation, like Germanic inheritance reckoning, shaped later counting. Gregory I, if the letter is truly his, let Anglo-Saxons rest at the fourth degree. Motives joined recognition of Roman prohibitions with extension beyond them. Calculation weighs line, degree, and stock: direct line counts generations, while Uniat Churches forbid collateral marriage to the seventh degree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-creighton-uni:
An institutional entry describes Creighton University at Omaha, Nebraska, conducted by the Jesuit Fathers. It comprised high school and college classes, a free classical day college, and schools covering medicine, dentistry, pharmacy, and law. In 1907-08 its faculty numbered 104, and attendance ran near 800.

Creighton ranked as the first free Catholic college in the country. Edward Creighton had planned a free school for higher education but died intestate before providing for it. His widow Mary Lucretia carried out his intention by a bequest near 200,000 dollars. The university's free dispensary and dental infirmary served thousands yearly, and its hospital treated about 2,400 patients a year, over half of them non-Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-moriart:
A biographical entry follows David Moriarty, Bishop of Kerry and pulpit orator, born at Ardfert in 1812 and dead in 1877. Schooled in his native diocese and at Boulogne, he passed to Maynooth, spent two years in the Dunboyne establishment, and served four years as vice-president of the Irish College in Paris. His success there won him the presidency of All Hallows missionary college in Dublin.

There his noble oratory, chaste, elevated, varied, and convincing, became famous. Made coadjutor of Kerry in 1854, he succeeded in 1856, building churches, schools, a diocesan college, and convents. His Allocutions to the Clergy show profound thought in oratorical style. A patriot in O'Connell's mould, he nonetheless denounced Fenianism strongly, running counter to popular feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-de-paul-unive:
An institutional entry traces De Paul University in Chicago from Saint Vincent's College, opened in September 1898. Archbishop Feehan wanted a Catholic college for young men on Chicago's North Side, and Vincentian priests incorporated Saint Vincent's in June 1898. Engineering courses began in 1906, and the university itself was incorporated on Christmas Day 1907 by ten Vincentian priests and five Catholic laymen.

Besides collegiate studies, De Paul offered mechanical, civil, and electrical engineering and special science work, with thirteen priests and six laymen on faculty. Under Rector McCabe from July 1910, it opened degrees to women through its 1911 summer school, attended by one hundred sisters and lay teachers. In spring 1912 the Illinois College of Law joined as its law department, adding 150 students to a total of 550.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deity:
A comparative religion entry treats the non-Christian notion of deity, reserving the Christian idea for the article on God. It opens with the word's roots: Sanskrit dyaus, bright sky, yielding deva, bright beings, and kin words from Zeus to Jupiter, Diana, and Juno. History's earliest documents already show religion long established, with deities adored and sacrifices offered beyond memory.

Sections trace several paths to many gods. Nature powers were made human in form. Heroes rose to godhead by apotheosis. Augustine saw Rome's many gods melt into one Jupiter. Politics added gods as tribes joined or conquerors displaced old gods. Language itself shaped divine names. The entry closes with early monotheistic traces in the Rig-Veda and modern anthropological theories of Tylor and Spencer, judging them against the facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duty:
Duty, as lexicographers define it, is something due, a service one is bound to perform or to shun. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds a second sense, the unique stir of conscience voiced in the words ought, bound, and moral obligation. When a person judges I ought to do it, the judgment is felt not as mere statement nor as mere preference. It presses as imperative and magisterial, with a feeling that drives toward action.

The entry analyzes this datum of conscience at length, moving from personal duty to duties toward God, neighbor, and civil society. Since God wills civil society for the growth of human nature, he wills the authority without which it cannot stand. Since lower animals cannot hold rights, no duties are owed to them, though duties to God touch them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ellen-whitty:
Ellen Whitty, in religion Mary Vincent, was a Sister of Mercy who planted the order in Queensland, born near Wexford in 1819 and dead at Brisbane in 1892. She was a chief helper of Mother Catherine McAuley in founding the Institute of the Sisters of Mercy. In 1839 she joined the young community in Baggot Street, Dublin, was trained by the foundress, became mistress of novices in 1844, and superior-general in 1849.

During the Crimean War she offered her nuns to nurse sick and wounded soldiers, and her sister Mary Agnes went to the front. In 1861 Bishop James Quinn of Brisbane, whose vast new diocese held only two priests and four churches, appealed for help. Mother Whitty led her sisters to Queensland, landing on 10 May 1861, and laboured there for the rest of her life, founding more than twenty convents before her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eternity:
Boetius defines eternity as the complete, succession-free possession of endless life. The definition, adopted by the Schoolmen for God's eternity, implies four things: a life without beginning, end, or succession, and of the most perfect kind. God not only is or exists, but lives. Applied to God, the notion of life, like every abstract notion, remains only analogous.

He does not live or exist precisely as anything else we know. Our notions of life and existence come from creatures, where life implies change and existence is added to essence. In God there can be no composition or change or imperfection, but all is pure act or being. The agnostic is not thereby justified in saying we can know nothing of God. Yet the agnostic, arguing this way, still thinks and speaks of Him as really as we do.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-falsity:
Falsity means a wilful perversion of truth, in words or in deeds. Its forms include counterfeiting, false weights, false measures, bribery, and forgery. Tampering with a will counts among its graver and more harmful instances. The article treats falsity as a sin against truth, justice, and neighbourly trust.

Canon law punished forgery of papal letters with excommunication. Pius IX renewed that penalty in his constitution Apostolicae Sedis. A person who profits by falsity must make full restitution in conscience. The article weighs excuses, ignorance, good faith, and the duty to repair harm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fordham-unive:
Fordham University in New York grew out of St. John's College, opened on Rose Hill Farm at Fordham on 24 June 1841 by Bishop Hughes. Its theological seminary had moved there the same year from Lafargeville, and the New York legislature gave it degree-granting powers in April 1846. Two months later the Jesuits bought the property from the diocese, and Augustus Thebaud became its first Jesuit president.

Early enrolment rose and fell with the times, dipping during the Civil War and reaching about 500 students early in the new century. A law school and a medical school opened in 1904 under President John Collins. By 1912 the university counted 548 students under 124 professors, spread across law, medicine, and the academic department, with its own press publishing historical work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaston-jean-b:
Gaston de Renty, a French layman born in Normandy in 1611, gave up court, army, and politics for the poor. Only son of Baron de Renty, he studied at the Collège de Navarre and the Jesuits at Caen, finishing at seventeen at the College of Nobles. He wrote treatises on mathematics, in which he excelled, before the Imitation of Christ turned his mind toward holiness.

Though he wished to become a Carthusian, he married at his parents' wish. In 1638 he left public life for works of mercy, teaching catechism to travelers sheltering at Saint Gervaise Hospital in Paris. With Henry Michael Buch he founded the Brother Shoemakers, honest workmen who shared earnings with the poor. Nine years after his death in 1649, his body was found intact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georgetown-un:
Georgetown University, in Washington, is the United States' oldest Catholic school of higher learning. Founded just after the Revolutionary War by Maryland's incorporated Catholic clergy, it chose trustees empowered to name a president and professors. It has stood under the Society of Jesus since 1805. Its chronicles reach back to earlier Maryland Jesuit schools, conducted by stealth under laws against Catholic education.

John Carroll, who had schooled at Bohemia in Cecil County, forms the moral and personal link to those schools and to Georgetown itself. He drew the plan, issued a prospectus seeking English aid, and chose the site at Georgetown, then chief borough of Montgomery County, Maryland. The college marked its hundredth anniversary with pomp in 1889 and keeps Founder's Day each January in Carroll's honor, with his portrait, missal, and letters among its treasures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hair-in-chris:
Hair and head-dress in Christian antiquity are surveyed here from catacomb paintings to the age of wigs, with texts and monuments as the only safe guide. Early Christians simply followed their times: short hair for men, waved tresses for women, curled and tiered by the late second century. Images of Christ kept long hair parted in the middle and the Virgin kept her veil.

Byzantine mosaics show medium hair cut square across the brow, with jewelled crowns for emperors and closed crowns for bishops. Barbarians let their hair fall free until councils from Patrick's synod of 456 to Rome in 743 forced clerics to cut theirs short. Later fashions run from shaven crowns and long curls to the cautious clerical wig, baring only the tonsure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heredity:
Heredity, the drift of offspring to resemble parents, is paired with change, the common variety that accompanies likeness. Two methods study them: the counting method, working in numbers. The method of Abbot Mendel of Brünn, whose lost notes promise most toward an answer, above all on return. In a splitting one-celled organism heredity is simple, since both daughter cells are parts of the parent cell; sexual breeding tangles it.

Weismann's germ-plasm theory holds that each one combines body plasm with germ plasm, set aside early, stored in the sex gland, undying. The article weighs this against regrowth, where a cut hydra or begonia cutting makes new ones, and finds the theory weakened. Darwin's pangenesis, saying bodily fragments gather in sex cells, rests on no evidence and demands vast works. Hering's hidden memory and legacy of acquired traits remain contested, wounds proving marks are not passed on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heroic-act-of:
The Heroic Act of Charity is a devout offering for the souls in purgatory. A Christian gives God all the good works of his lifetime and all the suffrages that may come to him after death. The act stands defined by a decree dated 18 December 1885 from the Sacred Congregation of Indulgences, confirmed by Leo XIII the next day. One may make it using a set formula or simply through an act of will.

Many who practise it place their merits in the hands of the Blessed Virgin, following the advice of the Theatine Father Gaspar Olider. She may then distribute them as she pleases. Though often called a vow, the act is really an offering and, unlike a vow, it can be revoked at will. A separate vow never to revoke it would probably bind, the entry explains, because a person can dispose of his own will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hospitality:
Hospitality, as the church teaches it, means welcoming guests with alacrity and kindness, since those who cherish guests receive Christ in their persons. The Council of Trent enjoined all holders of church benefices, secular or regular, to practise it as far as revenues allowed, following a duty frequently commended by the holy Fathers.

The burden falls chiefly on two classes. Bishops bear it as pastors of the people and as ancient administrators of the faithful's offerings: Gregory's fourfold division gave the bishop's household a portion expressly for hospitality. Religious, above all monks who renounced worldly goods to serve others, bear it as a work of mercy. The entry traces episcopal and monastic hospitality through canon law and custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humility:
Humility means lowliness or submissiveness, from the Latin humilitas, or as Thomas says, from humus, the earth beneath us. Applied to persons and things it can mean what is abject, ignoble, or poor, as in humble birth or a humble dwelling. It can also mean afflictions inflicted by others, when one person humiliates another by pain or suffering.

In its higher ethical sense, the virtue treated here, humility is a modest estimate of one's own worth joined with submission to others. Bernard defines it as a virtue by which a person knowing himself as he truly is holds a lowly view of himself. He willingly submits to God and to others for God's sake. No one else can humiliate a person in this sense; only the person himself can, and properly only with divine grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immortality:
By immortality people usually mean this doctrine: after death, the human soul lives on in endless conscious existence. Alongside the question of God's existence, it forms the greatest issue philosophy has to deal with. Rational psychology and the philosophy of religion claim it first, though it also brushes against other philosophical fields and a few natural sciences.

Some sort of future life has been believed in, it seems, nearly everywhere and always. Here and there individuals have rejected it, and some religions and philosophical systems clash with it logically yet still have followers. Still, views among different peoples as to the life beyond the grave may have been vague and inconsistent. Yet belief in a future existence seems so far hard to root out from the human race as a whole.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-immunity:
Immunity, from Latin immunitas, means freedom from a legal duty imposed on a person or property by law, custom, or a superior's order. Such freedom counts as a privilege, then, and obeys the same rules. Church usage gives the name to legal freedoms favouring holy places and holy things, Church property, and Church persons.

Look past the changing cases across times and countries to the principle itself: immunity is Church persons' and property's freedom from secular courts. This principle varies necessarily in application according to circumstances. In societies with strong ranks, for instance feudal society, immunities play an important part. In modern society, where men stand much more on a basis of equality, they are less useful. The strong central state power looks on them with disfavour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-individual-in:
Thomas Aquinas supplies the starting point for this philosophy entry: an individual is a being undivided in itself yet set apart from other beings. Individuality is then the set of traits by which a thing holds that unity and keeps its separateness. The entry asks what actually makes a thing an individual, a problem that has taxed the great schools of thought.

Metaphysics comes first, with the world seen as a crowd of distinct things, from stones and animals to men, each recognized as its own. Psychology follows, since mind and self raise the same question from within. The entry closes by noting what individuality means for ethics and for teaching. It is a compact guide to a wide question, not a verdict on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infallibility:
Freedom from error in final teaching on faith and morals is the claim this long theology entry defends for the Church. Infallibility here means a gift of divine help that guards the Church's definitive dogmatic teaching, not a promise that every churchman is always right. The entry lays out its case under five heads: what the claim means, its proofs, its organs, its scope, and which teachings it covers.

Its organs are ecumenical councils and the pope. Much of the entry weighs how the two relate. It tests hard cases from history such as Liberius, Honorius, Vigilius, and Galileo. Only strictly definitive sentences carry the guarantee, the entry stresses, while supporting argument in a judgment does not. Readers get the full Catholic case, with its limits stated as carefully as its claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infinity:
That which has no end, limit, or boundary is the idea this philosophy and theology entry explores. No finite measure, however often applied, can take in the infinite. No piling up of finite amounts can reach it. Taking finite amounts away cannot exhaust it. Though the word sounds negative, the entry argues it affirms the highest reality, since denying bounds, which are themselves negations, leaves a double negation.

Space and time give the term its first use, but it also applies to perfections such as wisdom, beauty, power, and fullness of being. The entry warns against mixing up infinity with “all-being,” since an infinite being lacks nothing that belongs to its perfection. Readers get a careful definition first, then the theological weight the idea carries in Christian thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-insanity:
No strict, fully satisfying definition of insanity exists, this entry admits at the start, since sanity shades into madness through a borderland that resists sharp lines. A definition that tries to be complete risks sweeping in states that are not madness at all, such as hysteria, fever delirium, or twisted passions. The Century Dictionary's wording is offered as about the best available.

That definition calls insanity a grave harm to the mind's powers. Those powers are intellect, feeling, and will, or one or more of them. Short-lived states caused by drink or acute fever fall outside it. Sorting kinds of insanity proves just as hard, since no single principle of sorting works cleanly. The entry weighs those problems for readers interested in law, morals, and medicine alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-inventory-of-:
A systematic list, item by item, of a person's or institution's goods, rights, titles, and papers is what an inventory means here, from the Latin inventarium. Law requires such lists to keep trustees honest: an inventory is drawn up when management begins. When it ends the outgoing official must produce everything listed or added since, except what was used up or worn out. An authorized official, a notary, or witnesses then check it.

Church property could hardly escape so useful a safeguard. The entry sets out how church rules adapted the civil practice to parishes, dioceses, and religious houses. Readers learn why a dull list matters: it fixes what a steward received, what he must hand back, and where gaps in the record point to fault.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irregularity:
A bar to taking holy orders, or to using orders already received, is what canon law calls irregularity, from a Latin root meaning not according to rule. Canons set the marks for lawful ordination. Those marks are moral probity, proper age, legitimate birth, and knowledge fitted to each order. They also include soundness of body, mind, will, and faith. A defect in any prescribed mark counts as an irregularity. Its direct effect is twofold.

First it forbids receiving orders, and second it forbids licit use of orders already held. Indirectly it also blocks a man who has become irregular from gaining a church benefice. Total irregularity bars every order and every use of orders, while partial forms bar only some. The entry sorts those kinds for readers who need the law behind a priest's fitness for office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irremovabilit:
Offices that cannot be taken away except for cause are the subject of this canon law entry, from a Latin root meaning not to be removed. Irremovability, or perpetuity, attaches to the chief church offices — pope, cardinal, bishop, parish priest — so that the holder keeps the post for life or for its set term. A pope may resign, while cardinals, bishops, and parish priests may resign or be removed only for cause.

Canonists held that a true canonical parish requires an irremovable rector. Exceptions exist, as when a rector holds only a vicar's charge for the true parish priest, and in some lands the bishop counts as parish priest of all. The entry focuses on parish priests, weighing when security of tenure protects a flock and when cause justifies removal. Readers get tenure law in miniature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kansas-city:
Kansas City was a Missouri diocese established on 10 September 1880, covering Missouri south of its great river and west of an eastern-county line, some 23,539 square miles. Suffragan of St. Louis, it began with forty-two churches, thirty priests, and twelve thousand Catholics. Its first bishop, John Joseph Hogan, transferred from St. Joseph and kept that diocese as administrator until separate jurisdiction was set up in 1893, when Maurice Burke took St. Joseph.

Hogan, born at Bruff in County Limerick in 1829, studied at the St. Louis seminary, was ordained in 1852, and was consecrated bishop in 1868 after building parishes across sparsely settled northwestern Missouri. Under him priests multiplied, churches rose, and new religious communities arrived. He asked for a coadjutor in 1896, and John Glennon served until his transfer to St. Louis in 1903. Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits, Lazarists, Redemptorists, and many orders of sisters worked in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kenraghty:
Kenraghty, also called Hanratty or Enright, was an Irish priest put to death at Clonmel on 30 April 1585. This entry follows him from study abroad and service as chaplain to the Earl of Desmond into prison, capture, and execution as a traitor.

Seized with the earl's fugitive party in 1583, he lay months in irons at Clonmel, teaching and hearing confessions through his cell grate. A bribed jailer let him out for one night to say Mass at a townsman's house, but soldiers ringed the house and seized the guests. Hidden under straw and wounded when the heap was probed, he slipped away, then gave himself up to save his host's life. He refused pardon for conforming, and his cause for canonization was under way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laity:
Laity, from Greek laos, the people, means the body of the faithful outside the clergy. The article treats the subject in three parts: the general idea, the duties and rights of the laity, and their privileges and restrictions.

Faithful stands against unbaptized outsiders, while laity stands against clergy. Both belong to one society but hold different ranks: clergy, raised by ordination into the sacred hierarchy, hold spiritual authority in government, teaching, and worship. The laity, left where baptism placed them, are governed, taught, and sanctified, the flock entrusted to shepherds and disciples guided by the apostles' successors toward eternal life. Such, the article holds, is the constitution Christ gave his Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-latin-literat:
Latin literature in early Christianity did not start in Latin at all. The Gospel's first Western preachers spoke Greek, and Greek ruled books, letters, and inscriptions. Irenaeus at Lyons refuted heresy in Greek. Clement's letter to Corinth was Greek, and Hermas's Shepherd, a Roman Church product, was Greek too.

Justin, Tatian, and Hippolytus all wrote in Greek at Rome, and popes' epitaphs stayed Greek down to 296. The oldest Latin document from Rome's clergy is their correspondence with Carthage during the vacancy after Pope Fabian's death in January 250. It includes a letter by Novatian, the first Christian writer to use Latin at Rome. In Africa, by contrast, Latin was always Christianity's literary tongue, from the Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs onward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-majority:
Majority, from the Latin majoritas, means the state of being greater or higher than another. Canon law gives it three chief senses. In voting, an absolute majority beats half the voters. A relative majority merely tops every rival. Special cases demand more, such as two-thirds for papal elections.

For persons, majority means reaching the age fixed for a given act. Twenty-one years is the common mark for civil life. In rank, it means the superiority that comes with office or dignity. That carries authority where jurisdiction is at stake. It carries deference where dignity alone counts. Clergy thus stand above laity, and clergy rank among themselves by jurisdiction and orders. Even churches hold precedence, from St John Lateran, mother and head of all churches, down through major basilicas and cathedral churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquette-uni:
Marquette University of Milwaukee grew from Marquette College, opened in 1881 though planned by Bishop John Martin Henni as early as 1850. In 1848, while in Europe, the bishop met Chevalier J. G. de Boeye of Antwerp, who gave sixteen thousand dollars toward a Jesuit institution in his far north-west diocese, first visited by missionaries Allouez and Marquette.

In 1855 Jesuits de Smet and de Coen arrived from Missouri to help the bishop, and St Gall's parish passed to Jesuit care. A charter came by special act in 1864, and Marquette College was dedicated on 15 August 1881. Robert A. Johnson's gift of a Grand Avenue building in 1907 let the college grow, its charter was amended, and it became a university. Milwaukee Medical College affiliated temporarily in 1907, Milwaukee Law School became its law college in 1908, and Applied Sciences and Engineering opened the same year. Economics followed in 1910, and a Music Conservatory in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-morality:
Morality means human conduct freely brought under the ideal of what is right and fitting. This entry distinguishes it from ethics, which is the science of that conduct. The ideal itself is broadly shared. Despite wide disagreement in ethical theory, peoples across time and place agree on the general lines of decent public and private behaviour.

Hobhouse is quoted to the point that comparative study ends by impressing the student with uniformity more than diversity. Rules of application differ sharply, as when some tribes hold filial piety to require ending aged parents' lives. The entry traces morality's sources in reason, custom and religion. It covers its relation to law and conscience, and how a common core survives beneath very different codes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-necessity:
Necessity, broadly speaking, means a tight link among distinct beings, among a being's parts, or between a being and its existence. It is a primary and fundamental notion, and fixing its various meanings and uses in philosophy and theology matters greatly.

In logic, the Schoolmen divided judgments into those in necessary matter and those in contingent matter. Judgments in necessary matter were called propositions per se, known to modern philosophers as analytic, rational, pure or a priori judgments. A proposition per se has a predicate that is either a constitutive element or a natural property of its subject, as with primary truths and metaphysical and mathematical principles. Kant's synthetic a priori, the entry argues, arose from ignoring the definition's second half. The entry then treats necessity metaphysically, physically and morally.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niagara-unive:
Niagara University, near Niagara Falls, New York, is conducted by the Vincentians. It was founded by John F. Lynch, later first Archbishop of Toronto, and chartered on 20 April 1863 as the Seminary of Our Lady of Angels. Fire destroyed the original building in December 1864, one wing of the present building rose in April 1865, and the structure was completed in 1869.

On 7 August 1883 New York's Regents erected the seminary into a college named Niagara University. A Buffalo medical school, existing from 1883 to 1898, furthered medical study and launched the movement requiring four years' study for New York's doctor's degree. In 1898 it merged into Buffalo University, as the Niagara law school had in 1891. The university now runs seminary, college and high school departments, with over 300 acres, a museum, laboratories, and a library of about 35,000 volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notoriety:
Notoriety, in canon law, means a fact so fully proved that judges may treat it as certain without further inquiry. The entry admits the word is hard to pin down, though lawyers use it constantly, and it sorts public, manifest, evident, and known into shades of proof.

Public means open to easy proof, manifest means known and held certain by many, and notorious means beyond dispute. The entry then divides notoriety of fact, of law, and presumptive notoriety, and traces their weight in trials and judgments. Authorities split it into notoriety of fact, of law, and presumptive notoriety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oregon-city:
Oregon City, an archdiocese west of the Cascades covering 21,398 square miles, grew from a joint Canadian and American mission. An 1836 indult joined the Oregon country to Red River's vicariate, and in 1838 Blanchet became vicar-general for Quebec and founded the first Catholic church in Oregon at Saint Paul in 1839.

Canadian settlers had built that church three years earlier, and De Smet arrived from Saint Louis besides. A vicariate of 1843 became a province in 1846, with Oregon City as archdiocese, and the entry follows its bishops, parishes, and schools. Canadian settlers had built that church three years before any missionary arrived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-personality:
Personality, in this Catholic Encyclopedia study, is the self that underlies a whole life. It sets out three tasks. First comes the physical make-up of personality under scholastic theory. Then rival concepts that clash with it, and odd states of consciousness judged by what they show about the self. The scholastic case starts from self-awareness, which perceives not only thoughts but the thinker behind them.

That self is substantial, permanent, and one. It outlasts changing moods, since memory itself proves the I of today is the I of yesterday. Later sections test the theory against rival views and strange cases, from automatic writing by highly nervous subjects to possession. Possession, the entry argues, is no true double personality, since the invading spirit moves a body it never informs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-of-the:
Philip of the Blessed Trinity, born Esprit Julien at Malaucène in 1603, was a Discalced Carmelite theologian and missionary. He took the habit at Lyons in 1621 and studied two years at Rome's seminary. In 1629 he sailed for the Holy Land, Persia, and Goa, where he became prior and teacher of philosophy and theology. After his pupils Dionysius and Redemptus were martyred in 1638, he carried their cause to Rome, though beatification waited until 1900.

He never returned to the missions, instead holding high offices in France and election as general of the order in 1665, with re-election three years later. A gale off Calabria on a visitation tour left him dying at Naples in 1671. Fluent in French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Persian, and Arabic, he wrote Thomist sums of philosophy, theology, and mysticism, an eastern itinerary, and lives of Carmelite saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poverty:
Christ did not damn holding worldly goods, nor even great wealth. He had rich friends. Yet Christ ever warned of the peril of riches, the thorns that choke the good seed of the word. Poor and ever on the road, He said the Son of man has nowhere to lay His head.

To the young man who asked what to do for life everlasting, He said to sell all he owned and hand the proceeds to the poor. The vow turns on leave. A religious does no wrong acting with no word to his superior when he can truly say the superior, knowing the facts, would back him. It is harder when the superior would wish to be told, though he would gladly assent. Then the man sins if leave is seen as a term of backing, and not if both agree on the heart of the act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-property:
In the word's current sense, a thing's proprietor, or owner, holds the full right to dispose of it, so far as law allows. The thing itself, the object of this disposal right, is called property, and the disposal right itself, ownership.  So long as the owner keeps within law's bounds, he may dispose of his property as he will.

Several persons may hold varied rights in one thing: one the substance, another the use, a third the usufruct. Of these, only the holder of the highest right is called proprietor. The tenant of tilled land and the lessee of a house are not proprietors, since they lack the highest right. The entry then defends private property from natural law. The present order demands it for person, family, and community alike, so reason postulates a natural right to gain private property, a line Aristotle sketches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quality:
Quality, in philosophy, is treated here in its strict sense. Loosely, the word covers whatever can be attributed to a subject of discourse. Strictly, it is one of Aristotle's categories, set apart from the other nine he lists. The eighth chapter of the Categories handles it, while the sixth chapter opens by defining it as that on account of which we say a thing is such or such.

Quality is thus the accidental form that fixes a subject in a special mode of being. It answers the question, of what sort is the thing, as Saint Thomas Aquinas notes, and it pairs with the term talis, of such a sort. Aristotle, Saint Thomas, Lorenzelli, Mercier and Nys supply the entry's sources. Readers meeting the categories for the first time find here a short, technical account of how philosophy sorts the ways a thing can be described.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quantity:
Quantity, from the Greek poson and the Latin quantitas, stands first among Aristotle's nine accidents in the Categories. This encyclopedia entry follows his long logical treatment in the sixth chapter. His list classifies predicates of a concrete, material subject, and, as its last two terms show, chiefly of man. Quantity therefore belongs less to ontology, the study of being, than to cosmology, the study of the material world. It presupposes matter.

In the Metaphysics, Aristotle describes the concrete quantum as that which divides into parts contained in it, each part potentially one thing itself. That description separates the unreal parts of a quantum from the elements of a compound, its matter and form. Saint Thomas, Lorenzelli, Mercier and Nys supply the modern sources, with notes on individuation and on matter and unending dimensions. Readers of Scholastic philosophy find here the companion piece to the entry on quality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reputation-as:
Reputation as property starts from ownership: a man indefeasibly owns what his own labour, material, and resources produce. In the same way his reputation, the outcome of meritorious activity, is his property. To strip him of it without adequate cause is formal injustice, graver or lighter with the harm done. That counts as a personal injury and a violation of commutative justice that burdens the wrongdoer with restitution.

Saint Thomas, weighing detraction against other sins, judged it less than homicide or adultery but greater than theft, since among external possessions a good name holds first place. Nor does wrongdoing simply forfeit the esteem a man has won. As a rule no money payment is owed for reputation as such, unless a competent judge has fined the slanderer, whose conscience must then obey the direction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-whitty:
Robert Whitty was an Irish priest who moved from the London hierarchy into the Jesuits and ended as a senior figure of the order. Born near Oylgate in 1817, he entered Maynooth at fourteen in 1830. Still too young for orders after extra years on the Dunboyne establishment, he offered himself to Dr Griffiths, who ordained him at St Edmund's, Ware, in 1840.

He sympathised with the Oxford converts and befriended Newman and Oakeley before their conversions. Wiseman made him provost of the new metropolitan chapter and vicar-general in 1850. In that role he published the pastoral From the Flaminian Gate, which English bigotry called papal aggression. Whitty later wrote that the cardinal never blamed him, though others did. In 1857 he resigned and entered the Jesuit novitiate at Verona. Back in England he taught canon law at St Beuno's, laboured in Scotland, and became provincial. He died in 1895 after 38 years as a Jesuit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rose-whitty:
Rose Whitty was an Irish Dominican sister and educator, born at Dublin on 24 November 1831 and died 4 May 1911. One sister became a religious of the Sacred Heart. Another joined the Dominicans and in 1870 led sisters to New Zealand, where she laboured until 1911. Rose entered St Catherine's Convent, Sion Hill, Blackrock, in her nineteenth year, on 25 March 1849.

Seventeen years later, at Bishop Moran's request, she and five others began work at Port Elizabeth on 23 November 1867. She led Rosemary Convent, her own foundation, as prioress for a quarter century. Her diamond jubilee of profession was celebrated in 1910, and a Mother Rose scholarship honoured her devotion to education. She kept good health until a month or two before her death, and was buried with public veneration at Emerald Hill Priory on 6 May 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacristy:
A sacristy is a room in or attached to the church where vestments, furnishings, sacred vessels, and treasures are kept, and where clergy meet and vest for ecclesiastical functions. It corresponds to the old secretarium or diaconicum. Almost everywhere now, the sacristy sits just behind the main altar or to one side.

It should hold labelled cases for vestments in every liturgical colour and a basin for washing hands. It should also hold a copy of Urban VIII's decree prohibiting certain offices and Masses, and a book of foundations and their fulfilment. Custom also calls for a font of holy water and a bell announcing the clergy's arrival at the sanctuary door. The sacristy is not blessed with the church and is not a sacred place canonically, though except for penalties it enjoys much the same prerogatives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-s-:
Saint John's University, a Catholic boarding school at Collegeville, Minnesota, run by the Benedictine Fathers of Saint John's Abbey, is the oldest Catholic college in the Northwest. Founded in 1857 by Archabbot Boniface Wimmer of Saint Vincent's Abbey in Pennsylvania, it began when Wimmer sent Demetrius de Marogna to Minnesota in 1856. He was to found a monastery and school in the diocese of Saint Paul. De Marogna came with two clerics, Cornelius Wittmann and Bruno Riss, and two lay brothers.

First called Saint John's Seminary, it took the name Saint John's University by an act of 17 February 1863. In March 1869 the state empowered it to grant college and university degrees. In 1878 Leo XIII allowed its president to confer doctorates in philosophy, theology, and canon law. It comprised a preparatory school, a high school, a school of commerce, a school of arts and science, and a seminary. It had 441 students in 1911-12.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sioux-city:
The diocese of Sioux City, erected on 15 January 1902 by Leo XIII, came wholly from Dubuque. It covers twenty-four counties in northwestern Iowa, 14,518 square miles. Sioux City stands on Iowa's far western edge, on the Missouri's east bank about one hundred miles north of Omaha. Next to Des Moines it is Iowa's largest city, with between fifty and sixty thousand people, set amid rich farm country where corn is the staple.

The diocese's Catholic population is almost sixty thousand, with 138 churches, 122 priests, 53 parish schools, four hospitals, and four academies. Parish schools hold 7,327 children. Its first bishop, Philip Garrigan, took possession on 18 June 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Christian Charity, also called Daughters of the Immaculate Conception, began at Paderborn, Germany, in August 1849. Pauline von Mallinckrodt founded the institute to teach poor schools and care for the blind. Her brother Hermann von Mallinckrodt was a famous figure of the time. The institute spread through Germany, then opened houses abroad.

In April 1873 the sisters founded a house at New Orleans and took charge of a parochial school. Mother Pauline soon established a new provincial mother-house at Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania. Their American houses eventually counted 668 sisters running 2 academies, 54 parochial schools, 2 orphan asylums, and 1 industrial school. Allowed back into Germany in 1887, they reopened the Paderborn mother-house and extended their work to Belgium and Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slavery-and-c:
This long survey asks what Christianity did for slaves and against slavery. It covers the Roman world first, then the world after the barbarian invasions, and last the modern world. Roman slaves were numerous and their lot hard, while slave labour crushed free labour. The missionaries came from Judea, where Mosaic Law treated slaves with mercy and secured labourers' wages, and where manual work carried no contempt.

The Apostles preached that in Christ there is neither bond nor free. Yet Paul drew no political conclusions and sought change through individual souls, asking masters to command with equity and slaves to obey without servile flattery. Early Christians freed slaves as alms, sometimes selling themselves to deliver others, and Gregory of Nyssa and John Chrysostom condemned slavery outright. Medieval serfdom replaced slavery in Christian lands, and the survey closes by crediting Christian teaching and charity as the principal cause of slavery's disappearance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society:
Society, this philosophical survey argues, means fellowship, not a herding of sheep or a hiving of bees. Its accepted definition is a stable union of many persons cooperating for a common purpose benefiting all, extending to mind, will, and outward faculties as the purpose requires. The definition comes from the Schoolmen, and the survey defends it against later confusion of man with beast, stock, and stone.

Authority stands as the first requisite of all society, since judgments differ on means and resolutions relax without headship. The survey then distinguishes artificial or conventional societies from natural ones, and treats the family as a natural society shaped by matrimonial purpose, mutual perfection, and the procreation and education of children. Social unions, it argues, are fenced by natural law guarding mankind's essential good.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-di: The Society of Divine Charity, in Latin Societas Divinae Charitatis, was founded at Maria-Martental near Kaisersesch in 1903. Its purpose was the solution of the social question through agriculture and trades, including printing, as well as through intellectual pursuits. The society brings together priests and laymen in a common program of manual work and study, joining farming and craft trades with learning as its answer to social needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sodality:
Sodalities are pious associations counted among confraternities and archconfraternities, and no sharp definition separates them from other confraternities. Their history matches that of religious confraternities, which grew rapidly from the end of the twelfth century with the great ecclesiastical orders. Some associations stood solely under the bishop, such as a peace association formed at Le Puy in 1183 under a carpenter named Pierre Durant.

This vast survey then traces particular sodalities across centuries and countries, from medieval prayer confraternities to modern archconfraternities. Among them are the Archconfraternity of Perpetual Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and Work of Poor Churches, conducted from Rome since 1879. Another is the Archconfraternity of the Most Holy Sacrament, raised in 1897, whose members keep a monthly hour of adoration. A Washington house has conducted the former in America since 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-solemnity:
Solemnity, in Catholic usage, names the degree of splendour with which a feast is kept, and this short encyclopedia entry unpacks the idea from its Latin roots. Intrinsic solemnity comes from the feast itself, such as a saint's birth, life, death, or relics honoured in a place. While extrinsic solemnity is added through holidays, ministers, decoration, bells, candles, and rich vestments.

Easter Sunday stands as the solemnity of solemnities in the Roman Martyrology, and the first Sunday of October holds the solemnity of the Rosary. The entry also notes how the word reaches beyond feasts into contracts, above all marriage. And into votive Masses, vows, and church trials, giving readers a compact guide to a term that turns up across liturgy and canon law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-faith-hop:
Faith, Hope, and Charity name two groups of Roman martyrs, long tangled together in legend. This entry works to tell them apart. One group is Sophia, Wisdom, with her three young daughters Pistis, Elpis, and Agape, martyred under Hadrian and buried on the Aurelian Way.

The other band, Sapientia with Spes, Fides, and Caritas, lies near St Cecilia in the cemetery of Callistus. Legends about both groups abound, yet early pilgrim guides and tomb-oil lists prove a real, ancient cult. Their Eastern feast falls on 17 September, and the Roman books keep Sophia with her daughters on 30 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tabernacle-so:
The Philadelphia Tabernacle Society, based at Notre Dame Convent, belongs to the Roman Association of Perpetual Adoration and Work for Churches. Five convent graduates began it in 1866 as the city's first Sodality of the Children of Mary, resolving to do work for the altar. Archbishop Wood affiliated it to the Brussels association in October 1878, and it joined the Roman arch-association in October 1881.

Twenty-two American societies now share that aggregation, and Philadelphia may affiliate parishes, which share all benefits. Over 10,000 members have enrolled since the start, with more than 1,800 active around the city today, and the approbation of 92 archbishops and bishops. It has aided about 4,600 parishes and missions, spending some 4,000 dollars a year on materials and giving away about a hundred sacred vessels yearly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-blessed-t:
Christianity's central doctrine receives its fullest encyclopedia treatment here, laid out in sections on Scripture, tradition, mystery, and Greek and Latin readings. The Trinity names the truth that within the unity of the Godhead stand Three Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, truly distinct yet one God, not three. The Athanasian Creed supplies the classic wording.

Scriptural proofs come first, drawn from both Testaments, then the witness of early writers and councils. Generation of the Son and procession of the Spirit are explained, with co-eternity and co-equality stressed throughout. Greek emphasis on the Father's monarchy and Latin stress on the Spirit's double procession close a demanding but lucid piece of dogmatic theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-bona-mors:
Dying well, in peace with God, was the aim of this confraternity, whose name means happy death. Vincent Caraffa, seventh General of the Society of Jesus, founded it on 2 October 1648 in Rome's Church of the Gesù. Innocent X and Alexander VII approved it, and Benedict XIII raised it to an archconfraternity in 1729, enriching it with indulgences.

Its longer title joins Christ dying on the Cross with Mary his sorrowful Mother, and devotion to the Passion forms its chief means. Members pursued a well-ordered life as preparation for death. The Jesuit father general directed it and could erect branches in Jesuit churches, a power Leo XII extended in 1827 to churches beyond the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-centre-pa:
Germany's Catholic political voice in parliament is the subject here, under the name Centre Party. It sat in the Reichstag from 21 March 1871 and in Prussian and state diets besides, with many members belonging to both Berlin assemblies. Prussia's lead in the empire made its statesmen imperial ministers as well, tying the two parties closely.

A predecessor, the Catholic Party in the Prussian Chamber, took the Centre name in 1859, though its roots reached a defensive group formed in 1852 against the Raumer decrees. Programme, leaders, and battles through the Kulturkampf follow, showing a party that defended church freedom while learning parliamentary politics. Elections, splits, and later fortunes round out the story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-leopoldin:
Vienna's answer to the needs of American missions is the subject here. When Lyons founded the Society for the Propagation of the Faith in 1822, it stayed French for years, and other nations debated whether to join it or start their own. Bishop Fenwick of Cincinnati sent his vicar-general, Father Rese, to Europe in 1827 to recruit German priests and seek aid.

Rese reached Vienna late in 1828 and won warm welcomes everywhere. Vivid tales of the New World, its promise for the Church, its shortage of priests, and its missions' poverty stirred public interest. A society on the French model soon took shape, named for Leopoldine, and began sending money and men across the Atlantic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-salesian-:
Boys of Turin, poor and neglected, found a father in John Bosco, whose Salesian Society takes its name from Francis de Sales. Its constitution opens with its object: Christian perfection of associates through spiritual and corporal works of charity toward the young, especially the poor, and education of boys for the priesthood. Valdocco's fields, then a suburb of Turin, cradled the institute.

Early nineteenth-century Italy, shaken by revolutionary philosophy, saw education, morality, and religion at their lowest ebb. From 1844 Bosco gathered boys for play, taught catechism, and heard confessions, building oratory, schools, and workshops. Growth across Italy and the world closes a warm account of youth work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-virginity:
Virginity is treated here in both moral and physical senses. Physically it implies bodily integrity, whose visible evidence exists only in women, and Catholic faith teaches that God miraculously preserved it in Mary even during and after childbirth.

Two elements compose it: the material element, absence past and present of all complete and voluntary delight, whether from lust or lawful marriage. The formal element, a firm resolve to abstain forever from sexual pleasure. Material virginity is not destroyed by every sin against the sixth or ninth commandments. Yet the resolve reaches beyond mere bodily integrity, or it might coexist with vicious desires and cease to be virtuous. Later sections ask whether virginity is a special virtue, and trace Christian virgins as a glory of the Church from the first ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wittenberg-ci:
Wittenberg is the Prussian Saxon city where Luther launched the Reformation from its university and castle church. Albert the Bear founded it after winning the land from Slavs and settling Flemish colonists near a citadel they called Wittenborg, white mountain. His son Bernhard founded the Ascanian Saxon dukes, and Albert II's Saxe-Wittenberg line made it capital, winning franchises in 1293 and electoral rank in 1356. The line died out in 1422, passing the land to Frederick the Warlike of Wettin.

Frederick the Wise opened Wittenberg University on 18 October 1502, funding it from All Saints' collegiate benefices, its canons as teachers. Luther joined its theology faculty and lectured on philosophy, then theology from 1509, and on 31 October 1517 nailed his theses against indulgences to the castle church. Wittenberg swiftly embraced his teaching, dropping private Masses in 1521 and adopting Lutheran worship in 1522, with Bugenhagen as first Lutheran pastor in 1523 and Melanchthon reshaping the university on humanist lines.
doe-osti-2574291-potential-impacts-of-dy: Dynamic electricity pricing in California got its impact study, and this DOE report covers load shapes and bills. The pages detail the elastic-demand analysis. The regulators get their numbers. The pricing was dynamic. The demand was elastic. The state was California.

doe-osti-2998965-exploiting-the-prism-fe: SBND's neutrino camera got its purity check, and this DOE report uses the PRISM trick. The pages detail the monitor data. The physicists get their numbers. The camera was SBND. The trick was PRISM. The numbers were physicist. The report was DOE's.
